description.en: Students conduct a treasure hunt (outdoors if possible, indoors if not) to find natural or "found" objects. They sort their findings into categories, create simple value cards describing why each item matters, and display them in a class "treasure gallery."
description.es: Students conduct a treasure hunt (outdoors if possible, indoors if not) to find natural or "found" objects. They sort their findings into categories, create simple value cards describing why each item matters, and display them in a class "treasure gallery."

20.label: 20 Minutes
20.bestFor: Tight schedules, younger students (K-1), daily scheduling
materials: Paper lunch bags — 20, one per student (or fold from newspaper, free)
Plain paper — 40 sheets, for value cards
Star stickers — 1 sheet of 100, for gallery walk voting
40 to 60 small found objects for the hunt — free, teacher gathers (leaves, bottle caps, buttons, spare erasers)

description.en: Ask: "What did Layla and her friends find in the garden? Did they pay for any of it?" Establish the question: can you find something valuable today that costs nothing?
description.es: Ask: "What did Layla and her friends find in the garden? Did they pay for any of it?" Establish the question: can you find something valuable today that costs nothing?

description.en: Students walk around the classroom (or school hallway/outdoor space) and collect 2-3 "treasures" — anything interesting they notice. Indoors: a pretty eraser, a leaf that blew in, an interesting paper shape. Outdoors: rocks, leaves, sticks, pinecones.
description.es: Students walk around the classroom (or school hallway/outdoor space) and collect 2-3 "treasures" — anything interesting they notice. Indoors: a pretty eraser, a leaf that blew in, an interesting paper shape. Outdoors: rocks, leaves, sticks, pinecones.

description.en: Back at desks, each student holds up their favorite find. Quick class sort: "Is it pretty? Useful? Interesting?" Teacher tallies on board.
description.es: Back at desks, each student holds up their favorite find. Quick class sort: "Is it pretty? Useful? Interesting?" Teacher tallies on board.

description.en: "Did any of these cost money? What makes them worth keeping?"
description.es: "Did any of these cost money? What makes them worth keeping?"

discussionQuestions: What did you find that surprised you?
Why is your favorite treasure valuable to you?
Would you trade it for a dollar? Why or why not?

30.label: 30 Minutes
30.bestFor: Standard class periods, grades 1-3, weekly scheduling
materials: Paper lunch bags — 20, one per student (or fold from newspaper, free)
Plain paper — 40 sheets, for value cards
Star stickers — 1 sheet of 100, for gallery walk voting
40 to 60 small found objects for the hunt — free, teacher gathers (leaves, bottle caps, buttons, spare erasers)

description.en: Review story. Set hunt rules: find 3 things you didn't buy and would want to keep. No living plants. No one else's belongings. Indoors: use "found" items in designated zones (teacher pre-places interesting objects around the room).
description.es: Review story. Set hunt rules: find 3 things you didn't buy and would want to keep. No living plants. No one else's belongings. Indoors: use "found" items in designated zones (teacher pre-places interesting objects around the room).

description.en: Students search and collect their 3 items.
description.es: Students search and collect their 3 items.

description.en: For each item, complete a value card: "I found a ___. It's special because ___. It would cost money to buy because ___. But I got it for ___ (free / found it)."
description.es: For each item, complete a value card: "I found a ___. It's special because ___. It would cost money to buy because ___. But I got it for ___ (free / found it)."

description.en: Students lay their items and value cards on their desks. Quick gallery walk.
description.es: Students lay their items and value cards on their desks. Quick gallery walk.

description.en: "What made the best treasure? Was it the rarest? The prettiest? The most useful?"
description.es: "What made the best treasure? Was it the rarest? The prettiest? The most useful?"

discussionQuestions: Could you sell any of these? How much would you charge?
What's something FREE in our neighborhood that people might not notice?
Is something free worth less than something you buy? Why or why not?
What did Layla's friends have that the garden GAVE them?

45.label: 45 Minutes
materials: Paper lunch bags — 20, one per student (or fold from newspaper, free)
Plain paper — 40 sheets, for value cards
Star stickers — 1 sheet of 100, for gallery walk voting
40 to 60 small found objects for the hunt — free, teacher gathers (leaves, bottle caps, buttons, spare erasers)

sayThis.en: "You're building an exhibition, like the friends did. Everything in it has to be free. Nothing you bought. Nothing anyone bought for you. Three to five things. And here's the trick — the best one won't be the biggest. It'll be the one where everything is different."
sayThis.es: "You're building an exhibition, like the friends did. Everything in it has to be free. Nothing you bought. Nothing anyone bought for you. Three to five things. And here's the trick — the best one won't be the biggest. It'll be the one where everything is different."

doneWhen.en: Three students picked at random have each named one thing they're hunting for.
doneWhen.es: Three students picked at random have each named one thing they're hunting for.

watchFor.en: Students who plan to grab five of the same thing. Ask them "what makes yours different from everyone else's?" before they go out the door.
watchFor.es: Students who plan to grab five of the same thing. Ask them "what makes yours different from everyone else's?" before they go out the door.

description.en: Review story. Pose: "You're setting up a Treasure Exhibition like the friends did at the end of Season 1. Your exhibition only has items that cost $0. What will you display?"
description.es: Review story. Pose: "You're setting up a Treasure Exhibition like the friends did at the end of Season 1. Your exhibition only has items that cost $0. What will you display?"

sayThis.en: "Three to five things. If you can carry it and it belongs to nobody, it counts. If it's alive, leave it where it is."
sayThis.es: "Three to five things. If you can carry it and it belongs to nobody, it counts. If it's alive, leave it where it is."

doneWhen.en: Every student is holding at least three items.
doneWhen.es: Every student is holding at least three items.

watchFor.en: The student with twenty items and the student with none. Give the collector a cap out loud. Ask the empty-handed one what they've walked past twice.
watchFor.es: The student with twenty items and the student with none. Give the collector a cap out loud. Ask the empty-handed one what they've walked past twice.

description.en: Students collect 3-5 items.
description.es: Students collect 3-5 items.

sayThis.en: "Five things on every card. What it is. Where you found it. Why it's worth something. What a store would charge for it. And why it's going in your exhibition."
sayThis.es: "Five things on every card. What it is. Where you found it. Why it's worth something. What a store would charge for it. And why it's going in your exhibition."

doneWhen.en: Every item has a card with all five lines filled.
doneWhen.es: Every item has a card with all five lines filled.

watchFor.en: "Because it's cool" as the reason. Push once: cool to who, and why? That single follow-up is where the thinking happens.
watchFor.es: "Because it's cool" as the reason. Push once: cool to who, and why? That single follow-up is where the thinking happens.

description.en: Each card: name, where found, why valuable, estimated "store price" if someone sold it, and why you'd display it in your exhibition.
description.es: Each card: name, where found, why valuable, estimated "store price" if someone sold it, and why you'd display it in your exhibition.

sayThis.en: "Set your desk up like a museum. Card next to the thing, not underneath it. Someone should get it without you saying a word."
sayThis.es: "Set your desk up like a museum. Card next to the thing, not underneath it. Someone should get it without you saying a word."

doneWhen.en: Every desk is readable from standing height.
doneWhen.es: Every desk is readable from standing height.

watchFor.en: Cards face-down or buried. The whole next step fails if the cards can't be read.
watchFor.es: Cards face-down or buried. The whole next step fails if the cards can't be read.

description.en: Each student arranges their items on their desk with value cards displayed.
description.es: Each student arranges their items on their desk with value cards displayed.

sayThis.en: "One sticker each. Put it on the most valuable thing in this room. You can't pick your own. And you have to read the card first."
sayThis.es: "One sticker each. Put it on the most valuable thing in this room. You can't pick your own. And you have to read the card first."

doneWhen.en: Every sticker is placed and every student is back at their desk.
doneWhen.es: Every sticker is placed and every student is back at their desk.

watchFor.en: Stickers going to friends rather than to items. Say up front that you'll ask three people to justify their choice, and then actually ask.
watchFor.es: Stickers going to friends rather than to items. Say up front that you'll ask three people to justify their choice, and then actually ask.

description.en: Students walk the room, place a star sticker (or make a check mark) next to the item they find most valuable. They may not choose their own.
description.es: Students walk the room, place a star sticker (or make a check mark) next to the item they find most valuable. They may not choose their own.

sayThis.en: "Flip your card over. What would a store charge for this? Best guess. Don't look anything up. Then swap with your partner and argue about any number that looks wrong." After the total goes up: "That's what this room would cost to buy. We didn't spend a thing."
sayThis.es: "Flip your card over. What would a store charge for this? Best guess. Don't look anything up. Then swap with your partner and argue about any number that looks wrong." After the total goes up: "That's what this room would cost to buy. We didn't spend a thing."

doneWhen.en: Every guess is on the board and the class total is written and read out loud.
doneWhen.es: Every guess is on the board and the class total is written and read out loud.

watchFor.en: Joke numbers, a million dollars for a leaf. Hold the line: it has to be a price a real shop could print on a label.
watchFor.es: Joke numbers, a million dollars for a leaf. Hold the line: it has to be a price a real shop could print on a label.

description.en: On the back of each value card, students write what that item would cost if a store sold it. Use best guesses — no looking anything up. Pairs check each other's guesses and argue any that seem far off. Then one recorder adds every guess on the board for a class total. Point at the number: "That is what our room would cost to buy. We spent nothing." Ask what makes an item valuable if the price tag is not the answer.
description.es: On the back of each value card, students write what that item would cost if a store sold it. Use best guesses — no looking anything up. Pairs check each other's guesses and argue any that seem far off. Then one recorder adds every guess on the board for a class total. Point at the number: "That is what our room would cost to buy. We spent nothing." Ask what makes an item valuable if the price tag is not the answer.

sayThis.en: "Count the stars. Which one won? Did it cost anything? So what made it win?"
sayThis.es: "Count the stars. Which one won? Did it cost anything? So what made it win?"

doneWhen.en: A reason for value that isn't price is written on the board.
doneWhen.es: A reason for value that isn't price is written on the board.

watchFor.en: The answer stalling at "it was pretty". Ask what made it pretty and where it came from.
watchFor.es: The answer stalling at "it was pretty". Ask what made it pretty and where it came from.

description.en: Count stars. Which item got the most? Discuss: "Did the most popular item cost money? What made it win?"
description.es: Count stars. Which item got the most? Discuss: "Did the most popular item cost money? What made it win?"

discussionQuestions: How is the value of a found rock different from the value of a rock you'd buy at a store?
What makes something a 'treasure' vs. just a random object?
Layla found a smooth stone. What made it valuable to her — and not necessarily to someone else?
Is there such a thing as a free resource that costs something? (Like a park — who pays for it?)
Name three free resources in our school or neighborhood that people overlook.
extensionIdeas: Start a class "nature collection" that grows over weeks — add one found item per student per week
Take photos of found treasures and create a digital class museum
Research: what did kids in another era (1800s, 1900s) use as toys and treasures? Compare to today

beforeClass.en: Walk the outdoor space. Check it's safe and that there's actually something to find. Bare asphalt? Use the recycling bin and classroom objects instead. Count your star stickers; you need one per student.
beforeClass.es: Walk the outdoor space. Check it's safe and that there's actually something to find. Bare asphalt? Use the recycling bin and classroom objects instead. Count your star stickers; you need one per student.

runningLongOrShort.en: Long: cut the Gallery Walk to a single lap, no discussion. Short: add a second hunt round with one target — find something nobody else will have.
runningLongOrShort.es: Long: cut the Gallery Walk to a single lap, no discussion. Short: add a second hunt round with one target — find something nobody else will have.

focus: Find and name 2–3 natural objects with a partner
Sort finds into simple groups: rocks, sticks, leaves
Draw a favorite find instead of writing
Words: treasure, find, sort
Find and sort 4–5 objects on your own
Make a value card with a frame: "This ___ matters because ___"
Tell why one item is special to you

Choose your own categories and explain them
Compare two finds on a value card
Set up a labeled gallery display

Curate the gallery with a written rationale

description.en: Students plant a seed (or simulate planting with a paper "seed" in a cup) and simultaneously start a "savings journal" that tracks a parallel question: if you save $1 every week, how much do you have in 4 weeks? 8 weeks? 1 year? Both timelines run side by side — the seed and the savings jar grow together.
description.es: Students plant a seed (or simulate planting with a paper "seed" in a cup) and simultaneously start a "savings journal" that tracks a parallel question: if you save $1 every week, how much do you have in 4 weeks? 8 weeks? 1 year? Both timelines run side by side — the seed and the savings jar grow together.

20.label: 20 Minutes
20.bestFor: Tight schedules, younger students (K-1), daily scheduling
materials: Paper cups — 20, recycled or brought from home, free
Plain paper — 80 sheets, 4 per student for the folded savings journal

description.en: Ask: "How long did Frances say it would take for a seed to grow?" (1-2 weeks.) "What if you put $1 in a jar every week — how long until you have $10?" Establish the parallel: seeds and savings both need time.
description.es: Ask: "How long did Frances say it would take for a seed to grow?" (1-2 weeks.) "What if you put $1 in a jar every week — how long until you have $10?" Establish the parallel: seeds and savings both need time.

description.en: Students draw a large jar on their paper. Inside, they draw 10 sections (coins or lines) representing 10 weeks of saving $1. Color in Week 1.
description.es: Students draw a large jar on their paper. Inside, they draw 10 sections (coins or lines) representing 10 weeks of saving $1. Color in Week 1.

description.en: Students write or say: "By Week 4 I will have $___. By Week 10 I will have $___."
description.es: Students write or say: "By Week 4 I will have $___. By Week 10 I will have $___."

description.en: "What's the hardest part of saving — getting the first dollar, or not spending it while you wait?"
description.es: "What's the hardest part of saving — getting the first dollar, or not spending it while you wait?"

discussionQuestions: Why was it hard for Riley to wait for her seed to grow?
Have you ever saved up for something? How long did it take?
What's the difference between spending money and saving it?

30.label: 30 Minutes
30.bestFor: Standard class periods, grades 1-3, weekly scheduling
materials: Paper cups — 20, recycled or brought from home, free
Plain paper — 80 sheets, 4 per student for the folded savings journal

description.en: Students draw their savings jar tracker: a jar with 8 rows labeled Week 1 through Week 8. Each row = $1 saved. "By Week 8, you'd have $8 — what could you buy with $8?"
description.es: Students draw their savings jar tracker: a jar with 8 rows labeled Week 1 through Week 8. Each row = $1 saved. "By Week 8, you'd have $8 — what could you buy with $8?"

description.en: Fill cups with soil. Make a small hole. Place seed. Cover gently. Label with name marker. Water lightly.
description.es: Fill cups with soil. Make a small hole. Place seed. Cover gently. Label with name marker. Water lightly.

description.en: Students complete two predictions: "I think my seed will sprout in ___ days" and "If I save $1 per week for 8 weeks, I'll have ___. I could use that to buy ___."
description.es: Students complete two predictions: "I think my seed will sprout in ___ days" and "If I save $1 per week for 8 weeks, I'll have ___. I could use that to buy ___."

description.en: Color in Week 1 on their savings jar. Date it.
description.es: Color in Week 1 on their savings jar. Date it.

description.en: "What do both your seed and your savings jar need? (Time and not messing with it.)"
description.es: "What do both your seed and your savings jar need? (Time and not messing with it.)"

discussionQuestions: Riley wanted to check her seed every hour. What happens if you spend your savings every week instead of letting it grow?
Frances said seeds make more seeds. What happens to savings if you add to it every week?
Is waiting easier when you can see what's growing? What if you can't see it yet?
What's one thing you could save for that would take 8 weeks?

45.label: 45 Minutes
materials: Paper cups — 20, recycled or brought from home, free
Plain paper — 80 sheets, 4 per student for the folded savings journal

sayThis.en: "Soil up to the line. Seed in. Cover it. One spoon of water — one. Too much water is how you kill it. Now draw your cup exactly how it looks right now, because in two weeks you won't remember."
sayThis.es: "Soil up to the line. Seed in. Cover it. One spoon of water — one. Too much water is how you kill it. Now draw your cup exactly how it looks right now, because in two weeks you won't remember."

doneWhen.en: Every cup is planted, labeled with a name, and drawn in the log.
doneWhen.es: Every cup is planted, labeled with a name, and drawn in the log.

watchFor.en: Flooding. One spoon means one spoon. Also the student who buries the seed at the bottom of the cup.
watchFor.es: Flooding. One spoon means one spoon. Also the student who buries the seed at the bottom of the cup.

description.en: Follow same planting steps as 30-minute version. This time, students also set up a "seed observation log" page in their mini-book — date, appearance of soil, drawing of cup.
description.es: Follow same planting steps as 30-minute version. This time, students also set up a "seed observation log" page in their mini-book — date, appearance of soil, drawing of cup.

sayThis.en: "Four pages. What you're saving for and what it costs. A chart with the first twelve weeks drawn in. One thing you could skip buying this week. And what a dollar a week gets you after a year."
sayThis.es: "Four pages. What you're saving for and what it costs. A chart with the first twelve weeks drawn in. One thing you could skip buying this week. And what a dollar a week gets you after a year."

doneWhen.en: All four pages have writing on them and page three shows a number of weeks.
doneWhen.es: All four pages have writing on them and page three shows a number of weeks.

watchFor.en: Goals of ten thousand dollars. Don't refuse it. Make them do the division and watch them find it themselves.
watchFor.es: Goals of ten thousand dollars. Don't refuse it. Make them do the division and watch them find it themselves.

description.en: Students create a 4-page savings section in their mini-book: - Page 1: "My Savings Goal" (what they're saving for, cost, how long at $1/week) - Page 2: A hand-drawn growth chart (weeks 1-12 filled in, rest blank) - Page 3: "What could I skip buying this week to save $1?" (list of small purchases they make or see family make) - Page 4: "What will I have after 1 year if I save $1/week?" (calculate: $52)
description.es: Students create a 4-page savings section in their mini-book: - Page 1: "My Savings Goal" (what they're saving for, cost, how long at $1/week) - Page 2: A hand-drawn growth chart (weeks 1-12 filled in, rest blank) - Page 3: "What could I skip buying this week to save $1?" (list of small purchases they make or see family make) - Page 4: "What will I have after 1 year if I save $1/week?" (calculate: $52)

sayThis.en: "Your seed turns into a plant in two weeks. Your savings turn into your goal in however many weeks you wrote down. What's the same about those two?"
sayThis.es: "Your seed turns into a plant in two weeks. Your savings turn into your goal in however many weeks you wrote down. What's the same about those two?"

doneWhen.en: Every pair has reported one similarity to the class.
doneWhen.es: Every pair has reported one similarity to the class.

watchFor.en: Pairs that finish in thirty seconds with "both take time". Push for a second one: both are invisible at the start, both fail if you dig them up early.
watchFor.es: Pairs that finish in thirty seconds with "both take time". Push for a second one: both are invisible at the start, both fail if you dig them up early.

description.en: Pair discussion: "Your seed will become a plant in 2 weeks. Your savings will become your goal in ___ weeks. What's the same about both processes?" Partners report one similarity to the class.
description.es: Pair discussion: "Your seed will become a plant in 2 weeks. Your savings will become your goal in ___ weeks. What's the same about both processes?" Partners report one similarity to the class.

sayThis.en: "Swap books. You're the auditor now. Three checks. Does the chart add up week to week? Do the weeks actually reach the goal? Is the cost realistic? You have to find at least one thing to question. That's the job."
sayThis.es: "Swap books. You're the auditor now. Three checks. Does the chart add up week to week? Do the weeks actually reach the goal? Is the cost realistic? You have to find at least one thing to question. That's the job."

doneWhen.en: Every book has an audit slip and one initialed revision.
doneWhen.es: Every book has an audit slip and one initialed revision.

watchFor.en: Auditors who write "looks good" to be nice. Reject it. Nobody hands the book back without one written question.
watchFor.es: Auditors who write "looks good" to be nice. Reject it. Nobody hands the book back without one written question.

description.en: Partners swap mini-books and become each other's auditor. The auditor checks three things and writes each on a scrap-paper audit slip: does the growth chart add up week to week, does the number of weeks actually reach the goal, and is the goal cost realistic. Auditors must find at least one thing to question. Books go back, and each student makes one revision and initials it. Ask: "Did your auditor catch something you missed?"
description.es: Partners swap mini-books and become each other's auditor. The auditor checks three things and writes each on a scrap-paper audit slip: does the growth chart add up week to week, does the number of weeks actually reach the goal, and is the goal cost realistic. Auditors must find at least one thing to question. Books go back, and each student makes one revision and initials it. Ask: "Did your auditor catch something you missed?"

sayThis.en: "Name and goal on the class sheet. This stays up all year. I'm going to ask you about it."
sayThis.es: "Name and goal on the class sheet. This stays up all year. I'm going to ask you about it."

doneWhen.en: Every name is on the sheet with a goal next to it.
doneWhen.es: Every name is on the sheet with a goal next to it.

watchFor.en: Students copying the goal above theirs. Ask them what they actually want.
watchFor.es: Students copying the goal above theirs. Ask them what they actually want.

description.en: On a large piece of paper displayed in class, everyone adds their name and their savings goal. Will check in monthly.
description.es: On a large piece of paper displayed in class, everyone adds their name and their savings goal. Will check in monthly.

sayThis.en: "Frances saved seeds for years. A dollar a week for ten years is five hundred and twenty dollars. What would you do with that?"
sayThis.es: "Frances saved seeds for years. A dollar a week for ten years is five hundred and twenty dollars. What would you do with that?"

doneWhen.en: Two or three students have answered out loud.
doneWhen.es: Two or three students have answered out loud.

watchFor.en: Nothing. This one is short on purpose. Let it land and stop.
watchFor.es: Nothing. This one is short on purpose. Let it land and stop.

description.en: "Frances has been saving seeds for years. What would a person's savings look like if they saved $1/week for 10 years?" (Answer: $520.)
description.es: "Frances has been saving seeds for years. What would a person's savings look like if they saved $1/week for 10 years?" (Answer: $520.)

discussionQuestions: Frances said: 'You start with something small. You wait patiently. Then you get something big.' How is this true for both seeds and savings?
If you check your savings every day, does it grow faster? What about if you add $2/week instead of $1?
What's the hardest thing about not spending money you have?
Benny chose sunflower seeds — the biggest kind. If you want to save MORE, what do you change?
What's one thing your family already grows, makes, or saves instead of buying?
extensionIdeas: Weekly seed observation logs maintained for the full growth cycle (photograph or draw)
Create a class savings chart on the wall that fills in each week for 8 weeks
Research: what does a savings account do with your money while you wait? (Interest — brief intro for T4)

beforeClass.en: Fill the cups with soil before students arrive; doing it live costs ten minutes and makes a mess. Decide now where the cups will sit for two weeks and whether that spot gets light.
beforeClass.es: Fill the cups with soil before students arrive; doing it live costs ten minutes and makes a mess. Decide now where the cups will sit for two weeks and whether that spot gets light.

runningLongOrShort.en: Long: drop the seed-vs-savings pair discussion and make it a whole-class question. Short: add a fifth portfolio page — "who could I ask to match my savings?"
runningLongOrShort.es: Long: drop the seed-vs-savings pair discussion and make it a whole-class question. Short: add a fifth portfolio page — "who could I ask to match my savings?"

description.en: Students bring 1-3 small items from home (pencils, stickers, small toys, trading cards, books) and set up a classroom trading post. Before trading, each student creates "value cards" for their items. They then trade using only negotiation — no play money, just agreement. The goal: end up with something you value more than what you started with.
description.es: Students bring 1-3 small items from home (pencils, stickers, small toys, trading cards, books) and set up a classroom trading post. Before trading, each student creates "value cards" for their items. They then trade using only negotiation — no play money, just agreement. The goal: end up with something you value more than what you started with.

20.label: 20 Minutes
20.bestFor: Tight schedules, younger students (K-1), daily scheduling
materials: Construction paper — 20 sheets, for the three token sizes
Plain paper — 40 sheets, torn into value card squares
Backup trade box — 25 spare classroom items, free (spare pencils, erasers, stickers, bookmarks, small notepads)
Teacher sends a note home one day ahead: bring one item you no longer use

description.en: Review: both people must agree. You can say no. A trade is fair if both people feel happy after. Demonstrate: teacher and student model a trade. "I'll trade you this red pencil for that eraser — deal?"
description.es: Review: both people must agree. You can say no. A trade is fair if both people feel happy after. Demonstrate: teacher and student model a trade. "I'll trade you this red pencil for that eraser — deal?"

description.en: Turn to partner on right. Make one trade offer. Both can accept or decline. If you both agree, swap. If not, each keeps their item.
description.es: Turn to partner on right. Make one trade offer. Both can accept or decline. If you both agree, swap. If not, each keeps their item.

description.en: Rotate 2 seats. New partner. New trade opportunity. "Can I offer you my ___ for your ___?"
description.es: Rotate 2 seats. New partner. New trade opportunity. "Can I offer you my ___ for your ___?"

description.en: One final rotation. After: "Raise your hand if you ended up with something you like better than what you started with."
description.es: One final rotation. After: "Raise your hand if you ended up with something you like better than what you started with."

discussionQuestions: Did you trade? Why or why not?
Did anyone say no to a trade? Was that okay?
What made a trade feel fair?

30.label: 30 Minutes
30.bestFor: Standard class periods, grades 1-3, weekly scheduling
materials: Construction paper — 20 sheets, for the three token sizes
Plain paper — 40 sheets, torn into value card squares
Backup trade box — 25 spare classroom items, free (spare pencils, erasers, stickers, bookmarks, small notepads)
Teacher sends a note home one day ahead: bring one item you no longer use

description.en: For each item, students make a value card: draw the item, write or dictate "This is a ___. I'd trade it for ___ because ___." The card helps others know what the student wants in exchange.
description.es: For each item, students make a value card: draw the item, write or dictate "This is a ___. I'd trade it for ___ because ___." The card helps others know what the student wants in exchange.

description.en: Each student arranges their items on their desk with value cards propped up or laid out — their "trading booth."
description.es: Each student arranges their items on their desk with value cards propped up or laid out — their "trading booth."

description.en: Students walk around and look at all items. They may NOT trade yet — just browse. Mental notes only.
description.es: Students walk around and look at all items. They may NOT trade yet — just browse. Mental notes only.

description.en: Free-form trading period. Students approach each other with specific offers: "I'll trade you my ___ for your ___ — deal?" Both must agree.
description.es: Free-form trading period. Students approach each other with specific offers: "I'll trade you my ___ for your ___ — deal?" Both must agree.

description.en: Sit in circle. Share: "I traded my ___ for ___ because ___." Anyone who didn't trade says why they chose to keep their item.
description.es: Sit in circle. Share: "I traded my ___ for ___ because ___." Anyone who didn't trade says why they chose to keep their item.

discussionQuestions: Was there something lots of people wanted? What happened to its 'trade value'?
Did everyone agree on what was worth trading for? Why not?
How is a trading post different from a store?
Ellis made a token system to make trades fair. Why did he need that?

45.label: 45 Minutes
45.activityName: The Full Trading Post (with Token System)
materials: Construction paper — 20 sheets, for the three token sizes
Plain paper — 40 sheets, torn into value card squares
Backup trade box — 25 spare classroom items, free (spare pencils, erasers, stickers, bookmarks, small notepads)
Teacher sends a note home one day ahead: bring one item you no longer use

sayThis.en: "Price your own stuff. Small or common is one token. Medium is three. Something nobody else has is five. Write it on the card. Be honest — if you price everything at five, nobody's going to trade with you."
sayThis.es: "Price your own stuff. Small or common is one token. Medium is three. Something nobody else has is five. Write it on the card. Be honest — if you price everything at five, nobody's going to trade with you."

doneWhen.en: Every item has a token value written on a card.
doneWhen.es: Every item has a token value written on a card.

watchFor.en: Whole booths of five-token items. Ask them which one is genuinely rarer than the others, and watch the prices move.
watchFor.es: Whole booths of five-token items. Ask them which one is genuinely rarer than the others, and watch the prices move.

description.en: Each student sets up their booth. For each item, they assign a token value: small/common = 1 token, medium = 3 tokens, something unique/rare = 5 tokens. Write values on value cards.
description.es: Each student sets up their booth. For each item, they assign a token value: small/common = 1 token, medium = 3 tokens, something unique/rare = 5 tokens. Write values on value cards.

sayThis.en: "Ten tokens each. Everybody starts the same. What happens after that is up to you."
sayThis.es: "Ten tokens each. Everybody starts the same. What happens after that is up to you."

doneWhen.en: Every student has ten tokens on their desk.
doneWhen.es: Every student has ten tokens on their desk.

watchFor.en: Tokens going straight into pockets. They need to be visible on the desk.
watchFor.es: Tokens going straight into pockets. They need to be visible on the desk.

description.en: Each student receives 10 tokens (start equal). Tokens represent relative worth, not money.
description.es: Each student receives 10 tokens (start equal). Tokens represent relative worth, not money.

sayThis.en: "A trade is fair when the tokens balance. Three for three. Or three for three ones. You can argue about the price — but you both have to agree before anything changes hands."
sayThis.es: "A trade is fair when the tokens balance. Three for three. Or three for three ones. You can argue about the price — but you both have to agree before anything changes hands."

doneWhen.en: One trade has been demonstrated in front of everybody.
doneWhen.es: One trade has been demonstrated in front of everybody.

watchFor.en: Blank faces. Do one trade at the front with a volunteer before releasing the room.
watchFor.es: Blank faces. Do one trade at the front with a volunteer before releasing the room.

description.en: Teacher explains: "To make a trade fair, the tokens must balance. A 3-token item trades for another 3-token item, or three 1-token items, or you can negotiate. Both people must agree the token balance is fair."
description.es: Teacher explains: "To make a trade fair, the tokens must balance. A 3-token item trades for another 3-token item, or three 1-token items, or you can negotiate. Both people must agree the token balance is fair."

sayThis.en: "Go. Agree the tokens before you swap. If you can't agree, walk away. That's allowed and it isn't rude."
sayThis.es: "Go. Agree the tokens before you swap. If you can't agree, walk away. That's allowed and it isn't rude."

doneWhen.en: At least half the room has completed one trade.
doneWhen.es: At least half the room has completed one trade.

watchFor.en: The loud trader cornering quiet students. Stand near them. Also the student who trades nothing; ask what their price would have to be.
watchFor.es: The loud trader cornering quiet students. Stand near them. Also the student who trades nothing; ask what their price would have to be.

description.en: Open trading. Students must negotiate token values before swapping items.
description.es: Open trading. Students must negotiate token values before swapping items.

sayThis.en: "Stop. Does anybody feel like they got a bad deal? Tell us the trade and we'll vote on whether it was fair."
sayThis.es: "Stop. Does anybody feel like they got a bad deal? Tell us the trade and we'll vote on whether it was fair."

doneWhen.en: One trade has been put to the class and voted on.
doneWhen.es: One trade has been put to the class and voted on.

watchFor.en: Nobody speaking. Ask instead: who got the best deal in this room, and why?
watchFor.es: Nobody speaking. Ask instead: who got the best deal in this room, and why?

description.en: Pause. Anyone feel they got an unfair trade? How do we decide? Class votes on one disputed trade — was it fair?
description.es: Pause. Anyone feel they got an unfair trade? How do we decide? Class votes on one disputed trade — was it fair?

sayThis.en: "Same rules. But you can re-price anything you've still got, based on what you just learned."
sayThis.es: "Same rules. But you can re-price anything you've still got, based on what you just learned."

doneWhen.en: At least three students have changed a price on a card.
doneWhen.es: At least three students have changed a price on a card.

watchFor.en: Prices that never move. Ask them directly: did anyone want it at that price?
watchFor.es: Prices that never move. Ask them directly: did anyone want it at that price?

description.en: Continue trading. Students may re-value their remaining items based on what they learned.
description.es: Continue trading. Students may re-value their remaining items based on what they learned.

sayThis.en: "Three columns. The item. What you said it was worth. What it actually traded for. Everybody puts up one row." Then: "Circle every row where those two numbers don't match."
sayThis.es: "Three columns. The item. What you said it was worth. What it actually traded for. Everybody puts up one row." Then: "Circle every row where those two numbers don't match."

doneWhen.en: Every student has a row and the board is sorted into went up, went down, never traded.
doneWhen.es: Every student has a row and the board is sorted into went up, went down, never traded.

watchFor.en: Students skipping the third column because their item never traded. That's a row too — write zero. It's the most interesting line on the board.
watchFor.es: Students skipping the third column because their item never traded. That's a row too — write zero. It's the most interesting line on the board.

description.en: Build a value board on the class board: item, tokens it was first worth, tokens it actually traded for. Every student adds one row. Circle every row where the two numbers differ. Ask the traders in those rows what changed their mind. Then sort the board: which items went up, which went down, which never traded at all. Ask why the untraded items did not move, and whether a thing is worth anything if nobody wants it.
description.es: Build a value board on the class board: item, tokens it was first worth, tokens it actually traded for. Every student adds one row. Circle every row where the two numbers differ. Ask the traders in those rows what changed their mind. Then sort the board: which items went up, which went down, which never traded at all. Ask why the untraded items did not move, and whether a thing is worth anything if nobody wants it.

sayThis.en: "Count your tokens in and out. Did you come out ahead? Now the real question. Is something worth anything if nobody wants it?"
sayThis.es: "Count your tokens in and out. Did you come out ahead? Now the real question. Is something worth anything if nobody wants it?"

doneWhen.en: Every log is totaled and two students have answered the untraded-items question out loud.
doneWhen.es: Every log is totaled and two students have answered the untraded-items question out loud.

watchFor.en: "Profit" being read as winning. Ask whether the person who traded nothing lost.
watchFor.es: "Profit" being read as winning. Ask whether the person who traded nothing lost.

description.en: Fill in trade log. Total tokens in and out — did you "profit"? Whole-class debrief.
description.es: Fill in trade log. Total tokens in and out — did you "profit"? Whole-class debrief.

discussionQuestions: Was it harder to trade something you really liked? Why?
Did token values seem 'right' to everyone? What does that tell us about value?
Mr. Mason said 'reusing things means nothing goes to waste.' How is trading better for the environment?
How is Ellis's token system like money? How is it different?
If one item was very popular, did its value go up? What does that remind you of?
extensionIdeas: Run a class-wide trading post for a full week — add new items Monday, trade by Friday
Compare barter to modern "Buy Nothing" groups or Craigslist Free sections
Research: what did people in ancient civilizations trade? What was the first known currency and why was barter replaced?

beforeClass.en: Count out ten tokens per student into cups or envelopes before the lesson. Doing it live burns five minutes and half of them end up on the floor. Decide your ruling in advance for a trade that goes wrong, because one will.
beforeClass.es: Count out ten tokens per student into cups or envelopes before the lesson. Doing it live burns five minutes and half of them end up on the floor. Decide your ruling in advance for a trade that goes wrong, because one will.

runningLongOrShort.en: Long: cut Trading Round 2 to four minutes and keep the value board whole; the board is where the learning is. Short: add a third round where students may only trade with someone they haven't traded with yet.
runningLongOrShort.es: Long: cut Trading Round 2 to four minutes and keep the value board whole; the board is where the learning is. Short: add a third round where students may only trade with someone they haven't traded with yet.

title.en: Map It! Classroom Expedition & Blueprint Challenge
title.es: Map It! Classroom Expedition & Blueprint Challenge

description.en: Students create a simple map of their classroom or school, mark "points of interest," and then lead a partner through an expedition using only their map as a guide. The activity builds on observation, planning, and the insight that curiosity — not money — unlocks discovery.
description.es: Students create a simple map of their classroom or school, mark "points of interest," and then lead a partner through an expedition using only their map as a guide. The activity builds on observation, planning, and the insight that curiosity — not money — unlocks discovery.

20.label: 20 Minutes
20.bestFor: Tight schedules, younger students (K-1), daily scheduling
materials: Chart paper — 2 sheets, for the class map

description.en: Ask: "Benny found an old map. What did it help him do?" (Find the creek. Go somewhere new. Discover things.) "Today you'll make a map of our classroom."
description.es: Ask: "Benny found an old map. What did it help him do?" (Find the creek. Go somewhere new. Discover things.) "Today you'll make a map of our classroom."

description.en: Students draw a simple top-down map of the classroom from memory — just the major shapes (door, windows, desks, board). No detail required. Label 3 spots with an X: one place that's always useful (e.g., the pencil sharpener), one that's interesting (a bulletin board display), one that most people overlook.
description.es: Students draw a simple top-down map of the classroom from memory — just the major shapes (door, windows, desks, board). No detail required. Label 3 spots with an X: one place that's always useful (e.g., the pencil sharpener), one that's interesting (a bulletin board display), one that most people overlook.

description.en: Swap maps with a partner. Can they find all 3 X spots using only the map?
description.es: Swap maps with a partner. Can they find all 3 X spots using only the map?

description.en: "What would happen if you went exploring without a map or a plan?"
description.es: "What would happen if you went exploring without a map or a plan?"

discussionQuestions: Did your partner's map make sense? What was missing?
Benny's friends didn't know the creek existed. What free things exist near our school that most people haven't noticed?
How is a map like a plan for a project or a purchase?

30.label: 30 Minutes
30.bestFor: Standard class periods, grades 1-3, weekly scheduling
materials: Chart paper — 2 sheets, for the class map

description.en: Students draw a map of the classroom AND the hallway outside (or the school common area). Mark 5 Points of Interest with symbols: a star for "most useful," a heart for "most interesting," a question mark for "something I've never looked at closely."
description.es: Students draw a map of the classroom AND the hallway outside (or the school common area). Mark 5 Points of Interest with symbols: a star for "most useful," a heart for "most interesting," a question mark for "something I've never looked at closely."

description.en: Students take their map and walk to at least 3 of their marked spots. At each spot, they write one entry in their Discovery Log: "I found ___. It's ___ (free / useful / interesting). I notice it because ___."
description.es: Students take their map and walk to at least 3 of their marked spots. At each spot, they write one entry in their Discovery Log: "I found ___. It's ___ (free / useful / interesting). I notice it because ___."

description.en: Back at desks, compare discovery logs with a partner. "Did you notice the same things? Different things? Why?"
description.es: Back at desks, compare discovery logs with a partner. "Did you notice the same things? Different things? Why?"

description.en: Teacher asks: "How many of you found something interesting you walk past every day?" (Expect hands.) "That's what Benny did — he found the creek. It was always there."
description.es: Teacher asks: "How many of you found something interesting you walk past every day?" (Expect hands.) "That's what Benny did — he found the creek. It was always there."

discussionQuestions: What did you discover that surprised you?
How is being curious a kind of resource? What does it cost?
What free things are in our school that new students might miss?
Benny had a plan (the map). How did having a plan make the expedition go better?

45.label: 45 Minutes
materials: Chart paper — 2 sheets, for the class map

sayThis.en: "Before you move, plan. Where are you going? What route? What do you think you'll find? Then draw the map with your route on it."
sayThis.es: "Before you move, plan. Where are you going? What route? What do you think you'll find? Then draw the map with your route on it."

doneWhen.en: Every planning sheet has a route drawn on it.
doneWhen.es: Every planning sheet has a route drawn on it.

watchFor.en: Drawing the room instead of a route. The line matters more than the picture.
watchFor.es: Drawing the room instead of a route. The line matters more than the picture.

description.en: Students complete an Expedition Planning Sheet: "Where will I go? What route will I take? What do I expect to find?" Then draw their map with a marked route.
description.es: Students complete an Expedition Planning Sheet: "Where will I go? What route will I take? What do I expect to find?" Then draw their map with a marked route.

sayThis.en: "You're hunting three kinds of thing. Something that's there but people ignore. Something free to use. Something you've never noticed. At every stop write it down — found this, worth this."
sayThis.es: "You're hunting three kinds of thing. Something that's there but people ignore. Something free to use. Something you've never noticed. At every stop write it down — found this, worth this."

doneWhen.en: Every log has at least three finds written in it.
doneWhen.es: Every log has at least three finds written in it.

watchFor.en: Students following each other. Send them in different directions by name if you have to.
watchFor.es: Students following each other. Send them in different directions by name if you have to.

description.en: Students explore solo using their map and planning sheet. They're looking for things that: (a) exist but people ignore, (b) are free to use, or (c) they've never noticed before. At each stop, write "Found: ___. Value: ___."
description.es: Students explore solo using their map and planning sheet. They're looking for things that: (a) exist but people ignore, (b) are free to use, or (c) they've never noticed before. At each stop, write "Found: ___. Value: ___."

sayThis.en: "Hand over your map and your plan. Not your log. Your partner has to find your best discovery using only what you drew. If they can't, your map wasn't clear enough. Write what you found on their sheet."
sayThis.es: "Hand over your map and your plan. Not your log. Your partner has to find your best discovery using only what you drew. If they can't, your map wasn't clear enough. Write what you found on their sheet."

doneWhen.en: Every planning sheet has a partner's note written on it.
doneWhen.es: Every planning sheet has a partner's note written on it.

watchFor.en: Whispered hints. Say it once: no talking, the map has to do the work.
watchFor.es: Whispered hints. Say it once: no talking, the map has to do the work.

description.en: Return. Pair with a partner. Give your partner your map and planning sheet but NOT your discovery log. They follow your map and try to find your top discovery. Can they? What did they find that you missed?
description.es: Return. Pair with a partner. Give your partner your map and planning sheet but NOT your discovery log. They follow your map and try to find your top discovery. Can they? What did they find that you missed?

sayThis.en: "Four maps, one page. Agree on one route that hits your four best discoveries in the fewest steps. Draw it. You get thirty seconds to present it."
sayThis.es: "Four maps, one page. Agree on one route that hits your four best discoveries in the fewest steps. Draw it. You get thirty seconds to present it."

doneWhen.en: Every team has one combined route drawn and has presented it.
doneWhen.es: Every team has one combined route drawn and has presented it.

watchFor.en: Teams arguing about whose map to copy. Give them the rule: the route wins, not the drawing.
watchFor.es: Teams arguing about whose map to copy. Give them the rule: the route wins, not the drawing.

description.en: Teams of four combine their four maps into one classroom guidebook page on a shared sheet. They must agree on one route that hits the four best discoveries in the fewest steps, and draw it. Each team presents its route in thirty seconds. The class votes on the clearest guide. Ask what made the winning one easy to follow — and whether their own solo map would have made sense to a stranger.
description.es: Teams of four combine their four maps into one classroom guidebook page on a shared sheet. They must agree on one route that hits the four best discoveries in the fewest steps, and draw it. Each team presents its route in thirty seconds. The class votes on the clearest guide. Ask what made the winning one easy to follow — and whether their own solo map would have made sense to a stranger.

sayThis.en: "One sticky note. Where you found it, what it is, and why somebody should go."
sayThis.es: "One sticky note. Where you found it, what it is, and why somebody should go."

doneWhen.en: Every student has a note on the class map.
doneWhen.es: Every student has a note on the class map.

watchFor.en: Duplicates of the same spot. Ask the second person what they saw that the first didn't.
watchFor.es: Duplicates of the same spot. Ask the second person what they saw that the first didn't.

description.en: Each student adds one sticky note to the class map noting their top discovery: "At [location] I found ___ — worth visiting because ___."
description.es: Each student adds one sticky note to the class map noting their top discovery: "At [location] I found ___ — worth visiting because ___."

sayThis.en: "Benny's map was drawn years ago. Was it still right? Was yours? What makes a plan stop working?"
sayThis.es: "Benny's map was drawn years ago. Was it still right? Was yours? What makes a plan stop working?"

doneWhen.en: One reason a map goes out of date is written on the board.
doneWhen.es: One reason a map goes out of date is written on the board.

watchFor.en: The answer stopping at "things change". Ask what specifically changed in this room.
watchFor.es: The answer stopping at "things change". Ask what specifically changed in this room.

description.en: "Benny's map was drawn years ago. Was it still accurate? Was your map accurate? What makes a plan stay useful or become outdated?"
description.es: "Benny's map was drawn years ago. Was it still accurate? Was your map accurate? What makes a plan stay useful or become outdated?"

discussionQuestions: How did having a plan change your expedition compared to just wandering?
Mr. Mason gave Benny a notebook so he could draw his own maps. Why is making your OWN plan important?
The stepping stones across the creek were 'stable' — meaning safe and trustworthy. What makes a plan stable? What makes it unstable?
Benny found the creek because he found a MAP, not because he bought anything. What else do people discover without spending money?
What would happen if you planned a purchase the same way you planned this expedition — making a map before spending?
extensionIdeas: Create a "School Discovery Guide" — a real map for new students showing the best free resources and interesting spots
Design a neighborhood map showing free recreation options (parks, trails, public art, libraries)
Comparison: what did early explorers use as maps? How did they navigate without GPS?

beforeClass.en: Walk the route yourself and set the boundary out loud before anyone moves. Decide which doors are off limits. Have the class map already on the wall.
beforeClass.es: Walk the route yourself and set the boundary out loud before anyone moves. Decide which doors are off limits. Have the class map already on the wall.

runningLongOrShort.en: Long: skip the partner guide step and go straight to the team guidebook. Short: add a second solo round where students must find something at eye level or lower.
runningLongOrShort.es: Long: skip the partner guide step and go straight to the team guidebook. Short: add a second solo round where students must find something at eye level or lower.

focus: Draw a simple map with a few landmarks
Lead a partner to one spot using your map

chapterTitle.es: El Puesto de Arte de Riley

description.en: Each student identifies one thing they're genuinely good at — not necessarily art, but anything — and creates a "skill card." In a structured Skills Fair, students spend time teaching their skill to a partner. The experience of being sought out for what you know generates the same "full inside" feeling Riley describes in the episode.
description.es: Each student identifies one thing they're genuinely good at — not necessarily art, but anything — and creates a "skill card." In a structured Skills Fair, students spend time teaching their skill to a partner. The experience of being sought out for what you know generates the same "full inside" feeling Riley describes in the episode.

20.label: 20 Minutes
20.bestFor: Tight schedules, younger students (K-1), daily scheduling
materials: Plain paper — 40 sheets, for passports and thank-you strips

description.en: "Riley thought her art wasn't good enough. But Ellis said it was valuable. Today we're all finding our own valuable thing. Think: what is ONE thing you're good at that other people might want to learn?" Give examples: counting fast, tying shoes, drawing animals, knowing dinosaur names, singing a song, folding paper.
description.es: "Riley thought her art wasn't good enough. But Ellis said it was valuable. Today we're all finding our own valuable thing. Think: what is ONE thing you're good at that other people might want to learn?" Give examples: counting fast, tying shoes, drawing animals, knowing dinosaur names, singing a song, folding paper.

description.en: Students draw and write their skill on an index card: "I am good at ___. I could teach someone to ___ in ___ minutes." Decorate if time allows.
description.es: Students draw and write their skill on an index card: "I am good at ___. I could teach someone to ___ in ___ minutes." Decorate if time allows.

description.en: Find a partner. Take turns: "My skill is ___. Here's a quick version of it: ___." (30 seconds each.)
description.es: Find a partner. Take turns: "My skill is ___. Here's a quick version of it: ___." (30 seconds each.)

description.en: "Did your skill feel valuable when you shared it? Did it feel different to GIVE it than to show it off?"
description.es: "Did your skill feel valuable when you shared it? Did it feel different to GIVE it than to show it off?"

discussionQuestions: How is your skill like Riley's art? How is it different?
Does sharing your skill make you have less of it?
What would happen if Riley had SOLD her art instead of giving it away?

30.label: 30 Minutes
30.bestFor: Standard class periods, grades 1-3, weekly scheduling
materials: Plain paper — 40 sheets, for passports and thank-you strips

description.en: Students think of ONE skill — specific and real, not vague. "I'm good at art" becomes "I can draw a realistic dog." Teacher models: "My skill is writing really fast. I can teach you a trick for holding your pencil."
description.es: Students think of ONE skill — specific and real, not vague. "I'm good at art" becomes "I can draw a realistic dog." Teacher models: "My skill is writing really fast. I can teach you a trick for holding your pencil."

description.en: Write/draw the skill card: name, skill, one-sentence description, quick drawing showing the skill in action.
description.es: Write/draw the skill card: name, skill, one-sentence description, quick drawing showing the skill in action.

description.en: Pair with a partner. Person A teaches their skill for 2 minutes. Person B tries it. Switch.
description.es: Pair with a partner. Person A teaches their skill for 2 minutes. Person B tries it. Switch.

description.en: Move to a new partner. Repeat teaching round. Notice: is it easier to explain the second time?
description.es: Move to a new partner. Repeat teaching round. Notice: is it easier to explain the second time?

description.en: Back in seats. Write or say: "After I taught my skill, I felt ___. My partner felt ___. My skill has value because ___."
description.es: Back in seats. Write or say: "After I taught my skill, I felt ___. My partner felt ___. My skill has value because ___."

discussionQuestions: Did anything surprise you about teaching your skill?
Did your partner's reaction change how you felt about your skill?
Ellis said Riley's art was worth showing people. Was he right? How did he know?
What happened when Riley's stand was almost empty — did she feel more or less full?

45.label: 45 Minutes
materials: Plain paper — 40 sheets, for passports and thank-you strips

sayThis.en: "Four lines. What the skill is. What you can teach me. What somebody needs to do it well. And the hardest part. That last one is what makes you a teacher instead of a show-off."
sayThis.es: "Four lines. What the skill is. What you can teach me. What somebody needs to do it well. And the hardest part. That last one is what makes you a teacher instead of a show-off."

doneWhen.en: Every student has a card with all four lines filled.
doneWhen.es: Every student has a card with all four lines filled.

watchFor.en: "I don't have a skill." Nobody gets to write that. Tying laces, calming a little brother, finding things — all skills. Name one for them if you have to.
watchFor.es: "I don't have a skill." Nobody gets to write that. Tying laces, calming a little brother, finding things — all skills. Name one for them if you have to.

description.en: Students complete a detailed skill card: Skill Title, "I can teach you ___," "To do this well, you need to ___," "Here's the hardest part: ___." This prepares them to actually teach, not just demonstrate.
description.es: Students complete a detailed skill card: Skill Title, "I can teach you ___," "To do this well, you need to ___," "Here's the hardest part: ___." This prepares them to actually teach, not just demonstrate.

sayThis.en: "Cards on desks. One silent minute. Walk and read. No talking yet — you're shopping."
sayThis.es: "Cards on desks. One silent minute. Walk and read. No talking yet — you're shopping."

doneWhen.en: Every student is back at their own desk and the room has gone quiet.
doneWhen.es: Every student is back at their own desk and the room has gone quiet.

watchFor.en: Talking. Hold the silence; it makes the next step faster.
watchFor.es: Talking. Hold the silence; it makes the next step faster.

description.en: Cards are placed on desks. Students do a 1-minute silent gallery walk reading cards — no talking yet.
description.es: Cards are placed on desks. Students do a 1-minute silent gallery walk reading cards — no talking yet.

sayThis.en: "Three rounds, five minutes each. Go to the person you want to learn from. Teachers teach. Learners fill in the passport. When I call time, you move."
sayThis.es: "Three rounds, five minutes each. Go to the person you want to learn from. Teachers teach. Learners fill in the passport. When I call time, you move."

doneWhen.en: Every passport has three entries in it.
doneWhen.es: Every passport has three entries in it.

watchFor.en: Popular students swamped and quiet students alone. Cap it at three learners per teacher and steer people by name.
watchFor.es: Popular students swamped and quiet students alone. Cap it at three learners per teacher and steer people by name.

description.en: Three 5-minute rounds. Each round: students move to one "teacher" they want to learn from. Teacher teaches; learner fills in their Passport. When the round ends, learners rotate. Each student teaches 3 people total.
description.es: Three 5-minute rounds. Each round: students move to one "teacher" they want to learn from. Teacher teaches; learner fills in their Passport. When the round ends, learners rotate. Each student teaches 3 people total.

sayThis.en: "Frances brought Riley flowers after the art stand. Nobody made her do it. Write a thank-you to one person who taught you something. Say what you can do now that you couldn't do an hour ago."
sayThis.es: "Frances brought Riley flowers after the art stand. Nobody made her do it. Write a thank-you to one person who taught you something. Say what you can do now that you couldn't do an hour ago."

doneWhen.en: Every student has written and delivered one card.
doneWhen.es: Every student has written and delivered one card.

watchFor.en: "Thanks, it was fun." Send it back. It has to name the thing learned.
watchFor.es: "Thanks, it was fun." Send it back. It has to name the thing learned.

description.en: After the market, teacher distributes "thank you" tokens (or has students write a compliment card for one person who taught them something). Discuss: "Frances brought Riley flowers after the art stand. What is that equivalent to in the Skills Market?"
description.es: After the market, teacher distributes "thank you" tokens (or has students write a compliment card for one person who taught them something). Discuss: "Frances brought Riley flowers after the art stand. What is that equivalent to in the Skills Market?"

steps.title: What Is This Skill Worth? (10 minutes)

sayThis.en: "Put a price on your card. What would you charge to teach this to one person for one hour? Then swap with your partner and argue. Too high, too low, why."
sayThis.es: "Put a price on your card. What would you charge to teach this to one person for one hour? Then swap with your partner and argue. Too high, too low, why."

doneWhen.en: Every price is on the board and the class total is read out loud.
doneWhen.es: Every price is on the board and the class total is read out loud.

watchFor.en: Everyone writing the same number. Ask whether the hardest skill in the room and the easiest are really worth the same.
watchFor.es: Everyone writing the same number. Ask whether the hardest skill in the room and the easiest are really worth the same.

description.en: Each student writes a price on their skill card: what would you charge to teach this to one person for one hour? Pairs challenge each other's price — too high, too low, and why. Then a recorder totals every price on the board. Point at it: "That is one hour of this room's time." Ask what makes one skill worth more than another, and whether the hardest skill to learn is always the most valuable.
description.es: Each student writes a price on their skill card: what would you charge to teach this to one person for one hour? Pairs challenge each other's price — too high, too low, and why. Then a recorder totals every price on the board. Point at it: "That is one hour of this room's time." Ask what makes one skill worth more than another, and whether the hardest skill to learn is always the most valuable.

sayThis.en: "Every different skill in this room, one list. Count them. That's what this room owns, and none of it cost a thing."
sayThis.es: "Every different skill in this room, one list. Count them. That's what this room owns, and none of it cost a thing."

doneWhen.en: The list is on the board and the count is written at the bottom.
doneWhen.es: The list is on the board and the count is written at the bottom.

watchFor.en: Skills getting merged to save time. Keep them separate; the length of the list is the point.
watchFor.es: Skills getting merged to save time. Keep them separate; the length of the list is the point.

description.en: Together, create a class list: "Our classroom's skills:" — tally each unique skill. "We have ___ different skills in this room. Together, we're worth ___."
description.es: Together, create a class list: "Our classroom's skills:" — tally each unique skill. "We have ___ different skills in this room. Together, we're worth ___."

discussionQuestions: Did you value your skill more or less after teaching it? Why?
What happened when multiple people wanted the same teacher? (High demand.)
Riley could have sold her art instead of giving it. Would the lesson have been the same?
What's the difference between a skill you can sell, a skill you choose to give, and a skill nobody wants?
What skill does your family have that saves them money? (Cooking, fixing things, growing food.)
extensionIdeas: Create a "Class Skills Directory" that students add to over the school year — resource for when someone needs help
Explore: what are the most valuable skills in different careers? How do you develop a skill into something people pay for?
Compare: Riley's art stand is free. A commissioned art piece costs money. What changed? When is it okay to charge for something?

beforeClass.en: Decide how you'll move the room for three rotations and say it before round one starts. Have a fallback skill in your pocket for the student who says they have none.
beforeClass.es: Decide how you'll move the room for three rotations and say it before round one starts. Have a fallback skill in your pocket for the student who says they have none.

runningLongOrShort.en: Long: cut the market to two rounds instead of three. Short: add a fourth round where students must learn from someone they've never worked with.
runningLongOrShort.es: Long: cut the market to two rounds instead of three. Short: add a fourth round where students must learn from someone they've never worked with.
