standard.description: The passport is folded from plain paper. Thank-you tokens are torn paper strips.
items: Index cards — 100, for skill cards
Plain paper — 40 sheets, for passports and thank-you strips
Pencils — 20
Crayons — 4 boxes, shared

lowCost.label: Basic Classroom
lowCost.description: The passport is folded from plain paper already in the room.
items: Index cards — 100, for skill cards

focus: Name one thing you are good at
Make a skill card (draw it)
Show your skill to a partner
Words: skill, good, teach, learn
Describe your skill in a sentence
Teach your skill step by step to a partner
Notice a skill you learned from someone
Vocabulary: skill, practice, teach, talent
Break your skill into clear steps to teach it
Give and get feedback at the fair
Explain how skills have value to others
Vocabulary: expertise, feedback, value, demonstrate
Plan a mini-lesson and teach it effectively
Evaluate which skills are most useful and why
Reflect on how skills can be traded or hired
Vocabulary: proficiency, specialization, market value, mentor

description.en: Students run a classroom savings simulation over the course of one week (or compressed into a single session). They "save" virtual or play coins into a class savings jar each day, practice counting and recording, then make a group decision about what to do with the accumulated total — mirroring the friends' debate in the episode.
description.es: Students run a classroom savings simulation over the course of one week (or compressed into a single session). They "save" virtual or play coins into a class savings jar each day, practice counting and recording, then make a group decision about what to do with the accumulated total — mirroring the friends' debate in the episode.

20.label: 20 Minutes
20.bestFor: Tight schedules, younger students (K-1), daily scheduling
materials: Construction paper — 20 sheets, brown and grey, for coin cutouts
Plain paper — 40 sheets, for the savings tracker
One jar or cup — free, any container in the room

description.en: "The friends found $4.73 in one week just by looking. Today you're going to count a jar of coins and figure out the total."
description.es: "The friends found $4.73 in one week just by looking. Today you're going to count a jar of coins and figure out the total."

description.en: Each group gets a pile of mixed coins. Sort into piles: pennies, nickels, dimes, quarters.
description.es: Each group gets a pile of mixed coins. Sort into piles: pennies, nickels, dimes, quarters.

description.en: Count each pile. Record how many of each. "We have ___ pennies, ___ nickels, ___ dimes, ___ quarters."
description.es: Count each pile. Record how many of each. "We have ___ pennies, ___ nickels, ___ dimes, ___ quarters."

description.en: Add up the total. Teacher checks with the class. Correct if needed.
description.es: Add up the total. Teacher checks with the class. Correct if needed.

discussionQuestions: Did the total surprise you? Were there more pennies or more dimes?
If you found 1 coin every day for a year, how much would you have?
What would you do with $4.73 — spend it, split it, save it, or buy something for the group?

30.label: 30 Minutes
30.bestFor: Standard class periods, grades 1-3, weekly scheduling
materials: Construction paper — 20 sheets, brown and grey, for coin cutouts
Plain paper — 40 sheets, for the savings tracker
One jar or cup — free, any container in the room

description.en: Each student draws or receives a savings jar tracker. Explain: "Each day this week, you'll save a different amount. Today is Day 1 — save 25 cents." Students draw a quarter in Row 1 and write $0.25.
description.es: Each student draws or receives a savings jar tracker. Explain: "Each day this week, you'll save a different amount. Today is Day 1 — save 25 cents." Students draw a quarter in Row 1 and write $0.25.

description.en: Run all 7 days in 8 minutes. Teacher calls out each day's "find": - Day 1: 25¢ (quarter near the vending machine) - Day 2: 10¢ (dime at the park bench) - Day 3: 3¢ (three pennies near the fountain) - Day 4: 5¢ (nickel outside the corner store) - Day 5: 50¢ (found in the wash at home) - Day 6: 35¢ (two dimes and a nickel) - Day 7: $3.45 (found a whole collection — big find!) Students record each day and draw the coins.
description.es: Run all 7 days in 8 minutes. Teacher calls out each day's "find": - Day 1: 25¢ (quarter near the vending machine) - Day 2: 10¢ (dime at the park bench) - Day 3: 3¢ (three pennies near the fountain) - Day 4: 5¢ (nickel outside the corner store) - Day 5: 50¢ (found in the wash at home) - Day 6: 35¢ (two dimes and a nickel) - Day 7: $3.45 (found a whole collection — big find!) Students record each day and draw the coins.

description.en: Students add up all 7 days. Compare with a partner. Correct answer: $4.73.
description.es: Students add up all 7 days. Compare with a partner. Correct answer: $4.73.

description.en: Read aloud the three options from the story: "Benny said SPLIT IT. Ellis said SAVE IT. Layla said BUY SOMETHING WE ALL SHARE." Class vote. Discuss why people chose differently.
description.es: Read aloud the three options from the story: "Benny said SPLIT IT. Ellis said SAVE IT. Layla said BUY SOMETHING WE ALL SHARE." Class vote. Discuss why people chose differently.

discussionQuestions: Did Day 7's big find change things? What if you'd spent the first $1.28 before Day 7?
Ellis wrote everything in his notebook. Why was that helpful?
Why did Mr. Mason's penny jar story change how the friends thought about their money?
If you save $4.73 per week, how much do you have in a month? ($18.92)

45.label: 45 Minutes
materials: Construction paper — 20 sheets, brown and grey, for coin cutouts
Plain paper — 40 sheets, for the savings tracker
One jar or cup — free, any container in the room

sayThis.en: "Four columns. Date. Amount. Running total. Where you found it. Ellis kept records — that's the only reason he knew there was four dollars and seventy-three cents."
sayThis.es: "Four columns. Date. Amount. Running total. Where you found it. Ellis kept records — that's the only reason he knew there was four dollars and seventy-three cents."

doneWhen.en: Every ledger has four labeled columns.
doneWhen.es: Every ledger has four labeled columns.

watchFor.en: Students who skip the running total. Without it the next step doesn't work.
watchFor.es: Students who skip the running total. Without it the next step doesn't work.

description.en: Students set up a personal ledger: Date | Amount Found | Running Total | How Found. Teacher explains: "Ellis kept records. That's how he knew you're not going to believe this — we have $4.73!"
description.es: Students set up a personal ledger: Date | Amount Found | Running Total | How Found. Teacher explains: "Ellis kept records. That's how he knew you're not going to believe this — we have $4.73!"

sayThis.en: "Thirty coins are hidden in this room. When you find one, write it down before you go looking for the next one. If it isn't in your ledger, it doesn't count."
sayThis.es: "Thirty coins are hidden in this room. When you find one, write it down before you go looking for the next one. If it isn't in your ledger, it doesn't count."

doneWhen.en: All thirty coins are found and every one is written in somebody's ledger.
doneWhen.es: All thirty coins are found and every one is written in somebody's ledger.

watchFor.en: Pocketing coins and recording later. Say the rule again mid-round. Also the student who finds nothing — steer them toward an untouched corner.
watchFor.es: Pocketing coins and recording later. Say the rule again mid-round. Also the student who finds nothing — steer them toward an untouched corner.

description.en: Teacher has hidden 30 "coins" (paper or play) around the classroom in advance. Students hunt for them. Every coin found gets recorded in the ledger immediately: where found, denomination, running total updated.
description.es: Teacher has hidden 30 "coins" (paper or play) around the classroom in advance. Students hunt for them. Every coin found gets recorded in the ledger immediately: where found, denomination, running total updated.

sayThis.en: "Pool everything. Sort by type. Count each pile. One person writes the totals. Then we check it — because a total nobody checked is just a guess."
sayThis.es: "Pool everything. Sort by type. Count each pile. One person writes the totals. Then we check it — because a total nobody checked is just a guess."

doneWhen.en: One agreed grand total is written on the board.
doneWhen.es: One agreed grand total is written on the board.

watchFor.en: Two different totals. Good. Make them find the error rather than telling them.
watchFor.es: Two different totals. Good. Make them find the error rather than telling them.

description.en: Class pools all found coins. Pairs sort by denomination and count. One recorder writes the totals on the board. Class verifies the grand total.
description.es: Class pools all found coins. Pairs sort by denomination and count. One recorder writes the totals on the board. Class verifies the grand total.

sayThis.en: "Three proposals. Split it equally. Save it four more weeks. Spend it on something everyone gets. Thirty seconds each. Then we vote."
sayThis.es: "Three proposals. Split it equally. Save it four more weeks. Spend it on something everyone gets. Thirty seconds each. Then we vote."

doneWhen.en: All three proposals have been heard and every ballot is in.
doneWhen.es: All three proposals have been heard and every ballot is in.

watchFor.en: Proposals with no detail. Split it how? Save it for what? Make them finish the sentence.
watchFor.es: Proposals with no detail. Split it how? Save it for what? Make them finish the sentence.

description.en: Teacher facilitates a formal "financial meeting" — three students make proposals (assign roles in advance or take volunteers): - "I move that we split the money equally." (Propose how.) - "I move that we save it for 4 more weeks and then decide." (Propose what goal.) - "I move that we spend it on something the whole class can enjoy." (Name what.) Class discusses pros and cons. Vote by written ballot (secret vote adds engagement).
description.es: Teacher facilitates a formal "financial meeting" — three students make proposals (assign roles in advance or take volunteers): - "I move that we split the money equally." (Propose how.) - "I move that we save it for 4 more weeks and then decide." (Propose what goal.) - "I move that we spend it on something the whole class can enjoy." (Name what.) Class discusses pros and cons. Vote by written ballot (secret vote adds engagement).

sayThis.en: "The winning plan gets a budget. Here's the exact total. Spend it down on paper — item, cost, what's left. You can't go over, and you can't leave more than a dollar sitting there."
sayThis.es: "The winning plan gets a budget. Here's the exact total. Spend it down on paper — item, cost, what's left. You can't go over, and you can't leave more than a dollar sitting there."

doneWhen.en: Two teams have read a complete budget out loud.
doneWhen.es: Two teams have read a complete budget out loud.

watchFor.en: Rounded numbers that don't add up. Make them show the running balance line by line.
watchFor.es: Rounded numbers that don't add up. Make them show the running balance line by line.

description.en: The winning proposal now gets a budget. Teams take the exact total the class counted and plan how to spend it down to the last cent on a scrap-paper budget sheet — item, cost, running balance. They may not go over and they may not leave more than a dollar unspent. Two teams read their budgets out. Ask which plan the class would actually vote for now that the money has real things attached to it.
description.es: The winning proposal now gets a budget. Teams take the exact total the class counted and plan how to spend it down to the last cent on a scrap-paper budget sheet — item, cost, running balance. They may not go over and they may not leave more than a dollar unspent. Two teams read their budgets out. Ask which plan the class would actually vote for now that the money has real things attached to it.

sayThis.en: "Write the decision in the class ledger. Now — did the vote surprise you? What changed people's minds once real things had prices on them?"
sayThis.es: "Write the decision in the class ledger. Now — did the vote surprise you? What changed people's minds once real things had prices on them?"

doneWhen.en: The decision is written in the ledger and two students have said what changed their thinking.
doneWhen.es: The decision is written in the ledger and two students have said what changed their thinking.

watchFor.en: Sore losers. Name it: the vote was close, and the other plan wasn't stupid.
watchFor.es: Sore losers. Name it: the vote was close, and the other plan wasn't stupid.

description.en: Record the winning decision in the class savings ledger. Ask: "Did the vote surprise you? What changed people's minds?"
description.es: Record the winning decision in the class savings ledger. Ask: "Did the vote surprise you? What changed people's minds?"

discussionQuestions: Ellis said 'we need to record this.' Why does writing down what you have matter?
What would have happened if the friends spent their first $1 before they found the rest?
Mr. Mason saved for a whole year. What does that take? What gets in the way?
You voted to ___. Does everyone feel good about the decision? What did you give up?
How is a savings jar different from a savings account? What's the same?
extensionIdeas: Run the class savings simulation for a real week — each day a student "deposits" a token (a real penny or a paper one) and the class tracks the running total
Research: what is a savings account? What is interest? How does a bank use your money while it's saving?
Calculate: if you save $4.73 per week for 52 weeks, what do you have? What could you buy?

beforeClass.en: Hide the thirty paper coins before students arrive and write down where, or you'll lose some for good. Decide whether the vote is secret ballot or hands — secret works better.
beforeClass.es: Hide the thirty paper coins before students arrive and write down where, or you'll lose some for good. Decide whether the vote is secret ballot or hands — secret works better.

runningLongOrShort.en: Long: cut the coin hunt to six minutes; the counting and the meeting matter more. Short: run a second hunt with fewer coins and a time limit.
runningLongOrShort.es: Long: cut the coin hunt to six minutes; the counting and the meeting matter more. Short: run a second hunt with fewer coins and a time limit.

standard.label: From Scratch
standard.description: All coins are paper. The teacher pre-cuts them or students cut their own.
items: Construction paper — 20 sheets, brown and grey, for coin cutouts
Plain paper — 40 sheets, for the savings tracker
Scissors — 10, shared in pairs
Pencils — 20
One jar or cup — free, any container in the room

lowCost.description: All coins are paper. Scissors, paper and pencils are already in the room.
items: Construction paper — 20 sheets, brown and grey, for coin cutouts
One jar or cup — free, any container in the room

focus: Add a coin to the jar each day
Count the coins with the class
Draw how full the jar is getting
Words: save, coin, count, more
Record the daily total on a chart
Predict tomorrow's total
Decide as a group what to save for
Vocabulary: savings, daily, total, goal
Track the running total and the days remaining
Calculate how many more days to reach a goal
Explain why saving steadily works

Model the savings plan and project the end total
Compare saving fast vs. slow to the same goal
Defend a savings strategy with your data

description.en: Teams receive identical sets of limited classroom materials and a challenge: build the tallest freestanding structure in a set time. Crucially, teams must draw a blueprint BEFORE building. The planning phase is non-negotiable. After building, they assess: what from the plan worked? What did they find around the room (or in the rules) that helped?
description.es: Teams receive identical sets of limited classroom materials and a challenge: build the tallest freestanding structure in a set time. Crucially, teams must draw a blueprint BEFORE building. The planning phase is non-negotiable. After building, they assess: what from the plan worked? What did they find around the room (or in the rules) that helped?

20.label: 20 Minutes
20.bestFor: Tight schedules, younger students (K-1), daily scheduling
materials: Masking tape — 1 roll, pre-cut into strips

description.en: Students draw a plan for their tower on one sheet of paper BEFORE touching the other materials. "What shape? How tall? How does it stand up?" Teacher models drawing a quick box-with-layers plan.
description.es: Students draw a plan for their tower on one sheet of paper BEFORE touching the other materials. "What shape? How tall? How does it stand up?" Teacher models drawing a quick box-with-layers plan.

description.en: Using only the remaining 2 sheets of paper and 1 strip of tape, build the tallest freestanding structure possible. No scissors. Structure must stand on its own for 10 seconds.
description.es: Using only the remaining 2 sheets of paper and 1 strip of tape, build the tallest freestanding structure possible. No scissors. Structure must stand on its own for 10 seconds.

description.en: Teacher measures each structure with a ruler or hand-widths. Tallest wins. Show blueprints: "Did your plan match what you built?"
description.es: Teacher measures each structure with a ruler or hand-widths. Tallest wins. Show blueprints: "Did your plan match what you built?"

discussionQuestions: Did your blueprint help you build faster or slower?
Mr. Mason said 'before you build, you need a plan.' Were the friends glad he said that?
What would you do differently if you had one more piece of paper?

30.label: 30 Minutes
30.bestFor: Standard class periods, grades 1-3, weekly scheduling
materials: Masking tape — 1 roll, pre-cut into strips

description.en: Teams of 2-3. Draw a blueprint together — must agree before touching materials. Assign roles: one person is the "builder," one is the "holder," one is the "checker" (does it match the plan?).
description.es: Teams of 2-3. Draw a blueprint together — must agree before touching materials. Assign roles: one person is the "builder," one is the "holder," one is the "checker" (does it match the plan?).

description.en: "Look at what you have. Can you build your plan with exactly these materials? You may NOT get more. This is your budget."
description.es: "Look at what you have. Can you build your plan with exactly these materials? You may NOT get more. This is your budget."

description.en: Build the structure using only the materials listed on the budget card.
description.es: Build the structure using only the materials listed on the budget card.

description.en: Structure must: (a) stand on its own, (b) be taller than 6 inches, (c) have a "roof" (something covering the top).
description.es: Structure must: (a) stand on its own, (b) be taller than 6 inches, (c) have a "roof" (something covering the top).

description.en: Each team shows their blueprint and their structure side by side. "What changed? What did you discover?"
description.es: Each team shows their blueprint and their structure side by side. "What changed? What did you discover?"

discussionQuestions: Were you ever tempted to grab extra materials? What stopped you?
The friends used an old blanket they found — they didn't plan for that. Did you find any 'surprise' resources?
Mr. Mason said they built the fort 'using only things you found.' How is your structure similar?
What was the most resourceful thing your team did?

45.label: 45 Minutes
materials: Masking tape — 1 roll, pre-cut into strips

sayThis.en: "Four jobs, and they're real. Architect decides. Builder builds. Inspector checks the build against the plan. Materials Manager tracks what gets used. If you're not the Builder, you're not touching the materials."
sayThis.es: "Four jobs, and they're real. Architect decides. Builder builds. Inspector checks the build against the plan. Materials Manager tracks what gets used. If you're not the Builder, you're not touching the materials."

doneWhen.en: Every team member is holding a role card and one member of each team has said their job out loud.
doneWhen.es: Every team member is holding a role card and one member of each team has said their job out loud.

watchFor.en: Everyone wanting Builder. Assign rather than let them choose, and say why.
watchFor.es: Everyone wanting Builder. Assign rather than let them choose, and say why.

description.en: Distribute role cards. Each person reads their role: - **Architect:** draws the blueprint, makes final decisions on design - **Builder:** main hands on materials - **Quality Inspector:** checks that the structure matches the blueprint; flags problems - **Materials Manager:** tracks what materials are used; ensures nothing is wasted
description.es: Distribute role cards. Each person reads their role: - **Architect:** draws the blueprint, makes final decisions on design - **Builder:** main hands on materials - **Quality Inspector:** checks that the structure matches the blueprint; flags problems - **Materials Manager:** tracks what materials are used; ensures nothing is wasted

sayThis.en: "Draw it before you build it. Materials Manager, list exactly what goes where. Nobody touches a thing until every name is on that blueprint."
sayThis.es: "Draw it before you build it. Materials Manager, list exactly what goes where. Nobody touches a thing until every name is on that blueprint."

doneWhen.en: Every blueprint is drawn, listed and signed by all four.
doneWhen.es: Every blueprint is drawn, listed and signed by all four.

watchFor.en: Teams building while drawing. Stop them. This rule is the whole lesson.
watchFor.es: Teams building while drawing. Stop them. This rule is the whole lesson.

description.en: Architect draws blueprint with team input. Materials Manager lists exactly which materials will be used for which part. Blueprint must be signed by all team members before building begins.
description.es: Architect draws blueprint with team input. Materials Manager lists exactly which materials will be used for which part. Blueprint must be signed by all team members before building begins.

sayThis.en: "Build the plan. Inspector — if it stops matching, call a deviation check. Then your team decides. Change the build, or change the plan. Either one's fine. Doing neither isn't."
sayThis.es: "Build the plan. Inspector — if it stops matching, call a deviation check. Then your team decides. Change the build, or change the plan. Either one's fine. Doing neither isn't."

doneWhen.en: Every team has a standing structure and a deviation check marked on their blueprint.
doneWhen.es: Every team has a standing structure and a deviation check marked on their blueprint.

watchFor.en: Inspectors going quiet because calling it feels like telling tales. Back them publicly the first time it happens.

title.en: Recipe Math: Cost Per Serving Challenge
title.es: Recipe Math: Cost Per Serving Challenge

chapterTitle.es: La Caja de Recetas de Frances

description.en: Students receive a simple recipe and a price list for the ingredients. They calculate the cost per serving of homemade food, then compare it to the store-bought equivalent. The gap between "homemade cost" and "store cost" is the lesson. Older students design their own simple recipe and calculate its economics.
description.es: Students receive a simple recipe and a price list for the ingredients. They calculate the cost per serving of homemade food, then compare it to the store-bought equivalent. The gap between "homemade cost" and "store cost" is the lesson. Older students design their own simple recipe and calculate its economics.

20.label: 20 Minutes
20.bestFor: Tight schedules, younger students (K-1), daily scheduling
materials: Plain paper — 40 sheets, students draw their own worksheet
Board markers or chalk — teacher supply

description.en: "Frances made bread for $2 that fed 12 people. A store muffin also costs $2 — but it feeds one person. Which is the better deal?" Establish: MORE food for the SAME price = better deal.
description.es: "Frances made bread for $2 that fed 12 people. A store muffin also costs $2 — but it feeds one person. Which is the better deal?" Establish: MORE food for the SAME price = better deal.

description.en: Teacher reads 3 scenarios; students circle "homemade" or "store-bought" as the better deal: - Homemade soup: $3 for 6 bowls = $0.50/bowl. Can soup: $1.50 per bowl. Which is cheaper? - Homemade cookies: $2 for 20 cookies. Store cookies: $4 for 20 cookies. Which costs less? - Homemade lemonade: 1 lemon ($0.50) + water + sugar ($0.25) = 4 glasses. Store lemonade: $1 per glass. Which costs less per glass?
description.es: Teacher reads 3 scenarios; students circle "homemade" or "store-bought" as the better deal: - Homemade soup: $3 for 6 bowls = $0.50/bowl. Can soup: $1.50 per bowl. Which is cheaper? - Homemade cookies: $2 for 20 cookies. Store cookies: $4 for 20 cookies. Which costs less? - Homemade lemonade: 1 lemon ($0.50) + water + sugar ($0.25) = 4 glasses. Store lemonade: $1 per glass. Which costs less per glass?

description.en: Go through answers. Discuss: "Was homemade always cheaper? Why might someone still buy from the store?"
description.es: Go through answers. Discuss: "Was homemade always cheaper? Why might someone still buy from the store?"

discussionQuestions: Frances's vegetables came from her garden — that made the bread cost less. What if you grew your own food?
"Even if homemade is cheaper, what does it cost that we didn't count?" (Time, effort)
Benny said this bread was better than store-bought AND cheaper. Do you think that's always true?

30.label: 30 Minutes
30.bestFor: Standard class periods, grades 1-3, weekly scheduling
materials: Plain paper — 40 sheets, students draw their own worksheet
Board markers or chalk — teacher supply

description.en: Display the trail mix recipe. "Today you're Frances — figure out if homemade is worth it. First, estimate: do you think homemade trail mix costs MORE or LESS than $1.50 per serving?"
description.es: Display the trail mix recipe. "Today you're Frances — figure out if homemade is worth it. First, estimate: do you think homemade trail mix costs MORE or LESS than $1.50 per serving?"

description.en: Students fill in worksheet: write each ingredient, its cost, add them up for total batch cost.
description.es: Students fill in worksheet: write each ingredient, its cost, add them up for total batch cost.

description.en: "Our batch makes 4 servings. How much does each serving cost?" ($1.10 ÷ 4 = $0.275 ≈ $0.28 per serving.)
description.es: "Our batch makes 4 servings. How much does each serving cost?" ($1.10 ÷ 4 = $0.275 ≈ $0.28 per serving.)

description.en: Write: Homemade = $0.28/serving. Store-bought = $1.50/serving. "How much do you save per serving?" ($1.22) "If your family makes this once a week, how much do you save in a year?"
description.es: Write: Homemade = $0.28/serving. Store-bought = $1.50/serving. "How much do you save per serving?" ($1.22) "If your family makes this once a week, how much do you save in a year?"

description.en: "What does homemade cost that we didn't add up?" (Time, dishes, shopping for ingredients.)
description.es: "What does homemade cost that we didn't add up?" (Time, dishes, shopping for ingredients.)

discussionQuestions: Was your estimate right? Were you surprised by how much cheaper homemade is?
Riley asked Frances 'how much does this cost?' Why is that a smart question?
Is homemade always better? Can you think of when store-bought might actually be a better choice?
Frances's vegetables were free from the garden. What's something your family grows or gets for free that could lower a food cost?

45.label: 45 Minutes
materials: Plain paper — 40 sheets, students draw their own worksheet
Board markers or chalk — teacher supply

sayThis.en: "These are real grocery prices. You're going to design a recipe on paper — something a kid could actually make — and work out whether it's a good deal. Nothing gets cooked today. Circle three things on the list you'd use."
sayThis.es: "These are real grocery prices. You're going to design a recipe on paper — something a kid could actually make — and work out whether it's a good deal. Nothing gets cooked today. Circle three things on the list you'd use."

doneWhen.en: Every student has the price list with three items circled.
doneWhen.es: Every student has the price list with three items circled.

watchFor.en: Students expecting to eat. Say it once, clearly, at the start.
watchFor.es: Students expecting to eat. Say it once, clearly, at the start.

description.en: Review price list together. "These are real approximate grocery costs. You're going to design a simple recipe — something K-4 could actually make at home — and figure out whether it's a good deal."
description.es: Review price list together. "These are real approximate grocery costs. You're going to design a simple recipe — something K-4 could actually make at home — and figure out whether it's a good deal."

sayThis.en: "Three to six ingredients, all off the list. It has to be real — something you'd actually eat. Write the amounts, not just the names."
sayThis.es: "Three to six ingredients, all off the list. It has to be real — something you'd actually eat. Write the amounts, not just the names."

doneWhen.en: Every recipe has between three and six ingredients with amounts.
doneWhen.es: Every recipe has between three and six ingredients with amounts.

watchFor.en: Recipes with one ingredient, or twenty. Hold the range.
watchFor.es: Recipes with one ingredient, or twenty. Hold the range.

description.en: Each student designs a simple recipe (3-6 ingredients from the list). Must be something real (a snack, simple breakfast, lunch item). List all ingredients and amounts.
description.es: Each student designs a simple recipe (3-6 ingredients from the list). Must be something real (a snack, simple breakfast, lunch item). List all ingredients and amounts.

sayThis.en: "Cost for each line, then add it up. Now the harder bit — how many servings does that actually make? Guess honestly."
sayThis.es: "Cost for each line, then add it up. Now the harder bit — how many servings does that actually make? Guess honestly."

doneWhen.en: Every sheet has a batch total and a serving count.
doneWhen.es: Every sheet has a batch total and a serving count.

watchFor.en: Pricing a whole bag when the recipe uses a spoonful. Ask how much of it they actually used.
watchFor.es: Pricing a whole bag when the recipe uses a spoonful. Ask how much of it they actually used.

description.en: Fill in cost for each ingredient, add for batch total. Estimate how many servings the recipe makes.
description.es: Fill in cost for each ingredient, add for batch total. Estimate how many servings the recipe makes.

sayThis.en: "Total divided by servings. Write it big. That's the number that matters."
sayThis.es: "Total divided by servings. Write it big. That's the number that matters."

doneWhen.en: Every student has a cost per serving written clearly.
doneWhen.es: Every student has a cost per serving written clearly.

watchFor.en: Division errors that make snacks cost eleven dollars. Get a partner to check anything that looks strange.
watchFor.es: Division errors that make snacks cost eleven dollars. Get a partner to check anything that looks strange.

description.en: Divide total cost by number of servings. Write it clearly.
description.es: Divide total cost by number of servings. Write it clearly.

sayThis.en: "What does the store version cost? Work out what you save per serving. Then times it by fifty-two."
sayThis.es: "What does the store version cost? Work out what you save per serving. Then times it by fifty-two."

doneWhen.en: Every sheet has a saving per serving and a yearly figure.
doneWhen.es: Every sheet has a saving per serving and a yearly figure.

watchFor.en: Wild store prices. Anchor them with two real examples.
watchFor.es: Wild store prices. Anchor them with two real examples.

description.en: What would the store equivalent cost? (Teacher provides examples or students estimate.) Calculate the savings per serving. Calculate the annual savings if made weekly.
description.es: What would the store equivalent cost? (Teacher provides examples or students estimate.) Calculate the savings per serving. Calculate the annual savings if made weekly.

sayThis.en: "New rule. Your recipe has to come in under the target now. Swap an ingredient, cut an amount, or stretch the servings. Redo the math. Your partner checks it."
sayThis.es: "New rule. Your recipe has to come in under the target now. Swap an ingredient, cut an amount, or stretch the servings. Redo the math. Your partner checks it."

doneWhen.en: Every student is under the target and a partner has initialed the new math.
doneWhen.es: Every student is under the target and a partner has initialed the new math.

watchFor.en: Stretching servings to twenty to hit the number. Ask whether that serving is still a real portion.
watchFor.es: Stretching servings to twenty to hit the number. Ask whether that serving is still a real portion.

description.en: Teacher names a target: your recipe now has to come in under a set cost per serving. Students redesign on paper — swap an ingredient, cut an amount, or stretch the servings — and recalculate. Nothing is cooked or brought in; this is all arithmetic on the price list. Partners check each other's new math. Ask what the recipe lost when it got cheaper, and whether it was worth the saving.
description.es: Teacher names a target: your recipe now has to come in under a set cost per serving. Students redesign on paper — swap an ingredient, cut an amount, or stretch the servings — and recalculate. Nothing is cooked or brought in; this is all arithmetic on the price list. Partners check each other's new math. Ask what the recipe lost when it got cheaper, and whether it was worth the saving.

sayThis.en: "One sentence. Mine costs this per serving, the store costs that, I save this, and in a year that's this. Then tell us what your recipe lost when it got cheaper."
sayThis.es: "One sentence. Mine costs this per serving, the store costs that, I save this, and in a year that's this. Then tell us what your recipe lost when it got cheaper."

doneWhen.en: Every student has presented and their trade-off is written on their sheet.
doneWhen.es: Every student has presented and their trade-off is written on their sheet.

watchFor.en: Presentations that skip the last part. That's the interesting half.
watchFor.es: Presentations that skip the last part. That's the interesting half.

description.en: Each student (or pair) presents their recipe in one sentence: "My [recipe] costs $[X] per serving. The store version costs $[Y]. I save $[Z] per serving. In a year, that's $[A]."
description.es: Each student (or pair) presents their recipe in one sentence: "My [recipe] costs $[X] per serving. The store version costs $[Y]. I save $[Z] per serving. In a year, that's $[A]."

discussionQuestions: Did any recipe surprise you — either cheaper or more expensive than you expected?
Frances used vegetables from her garden (free). If you grew one ingredient, how does that change your math?
Benny said the bread was better than store-bought. Is 'better' part of the math? (Satisfaction has value too.)
What's the tradeoff for a recipe that saves $1.22/serving? Is it always worth it?
What's one thing your family makes at home that saves money? Do you know how much it saves?
extensionIdeas: Grocery store field trip or virtual grocery tour: find the cheapest version of 5 items on the price list
Create a "Class Cookbook" of the cheapest recipes designed in this activity
Research: what percentage of American food spending is on restaurants vs. groceries? What's the math behind eating at home?

description.en: Each student receives a "broken" item (a deliberately torn, crumpled, or damaged paper object) and a small set of repair tools (tape, glue stick, scissors, scrap paper). They diagnose the problem, decide on a repair approach, fix it, and then calculate: what would it cost to replace this vs. repair it? The activity builds both hands-on competence and a repair-vs-replace decision-making habit.
description.es: Each student receives a "broken" item (a deliberately torn, crumpled, or damaged paper object) and a small set of repair tools (tape, glue stick, scissors, scrap paper). They diagnose the problem, decide on a repair approach, fix it, and then calculate: what would it cost to replace this vs. repair it? The activity builds both hands-on competence and a repair-vs-replace decision-making habit.

materials: Plain paper — 60 sheets, teacher pre-tears the damaged items

description.es: Each student receives their torn card. "In the story, Benny's train broke in half. Your item has a problem too. BEFORE you fix it — diagnose it. What's wrong with it?"

description.en: Using only the tape strip provided, repair the item as well as possible. It should be flat, look as good as possible, and hold together when gently bent.
description.es: Using only the tape strip provided, repair the item as well as possible. It should be flat, look as good as possible, and hold together when gently bent.

description.en: Teacher holds up a new index card. "A pack of index cards costs $3 for 100 cards — about 3 cents each. How much did your repair cost?" (Almost nothing — just a piece of tape.) "What did you save?"
description.es: Teacher holds up a new index card. "A pack of index cards costs $3 for 100 cards — about 3 cents each. How much did your repair cost?" (Almost nothing — just a piece of tape.) "What did you save?"

discussionQuestions: Was the repair worth it? Why or why not?
Mr. Mason fixed Benny's train instead of buying a new one. Why was that smarter?
What things do you own that could be fixed instead of replaced?

30.label: 30 Minutes

materials: Plain paper — 60 sheets, teacher pre-tears the damaged items

description.en: Students receive all 4 broken items. Before touching any repair tools: write/draw what's wrong with each item on the back (one word per item: torn, wrinkled, cut, bent).
description.es: Students receive all 4 broken items. Before touching any repair tools: write/draw what's wrong with each item on the back (one word per item: torn, wrinkled, cut, bent).

description.en: Students work through all 4 repairs using only their toolkit. Challenge: make each item as close to "new" as possible.
description.es: Students work through all 4 repairs using only their toolkit. Challenge: make each item as close to "new" as possible.

description.en: For each item, complete the chart: | Item | What I used to fix it | Cost to fix | Cost to replace | Money saved | Teacher provides replacement costs: index card = $0.03, book = $5-15, frame = $10-20.
description.es: For each item, complete the chart: | Item | What I used to fix it | Cost to fix | Cost to replace | Money saved | Teacher provides replacement costs: index card = $0.03, book = $5-15, frame = $10-20.

description.en: "Which repair saved the most money? Which was hardest? Would you always repair instead of replace?"
description.es: "Which repair saved the most money? Which was hardest? Would you always repair instead of replace?"

sayThis.es: "Nobody touches a tool yet. All four items, in writing. What's broken. How it broke. Which tool fixes it. Mr. Mason always worked out the problem before he picked anything up."

doneWhen.es: All four rows are filled for every student, failures included.

watchFor.en: Blank rows for failures. Those rows matter most.
watchFor.es: Blank rows for failures. Those rows matter most.

description.en: Fill in full worksheet for all 4 items. Calculate total cost to fix vs. total replacement cost vs. total savings.
description.es: Fill in full worksheet for all 4 items. Calculate total cost to fix vs. total replacement cost vs. total savings.

sayThis.en: "Repairs cost time, not just tape. How long did each one take? Pick an hourly rate for yourself. Now work out what each repair really cost — materials plus your time. Circle every one that cost more than just buying a new one."
sayThis.es: "Repairs cost time, not just tape. How long did each one take? Pick an hourly rate for yourself. Now work out what each repair really cost — materials plus your time. Circle every one that cost more than just buying a new one."

doneWhen.en: Every student has a real cost per repair and at least one circle on their sheet.
doneWhen.es: Every student has a real cost per repair and at least one circle on their sheet.

watchFor.en: Rates of a hundred dollars an hour. Ask what somebody who does this all day would actually earn.
watchFor.es: Rates of a hundred dollars an hour. Ask what somebody who does this all day would actually earn.

description.en: Repairs cost time, not just tape. Students time-stamp each of their four repairs from their report, pick an hourly rate for their own labor, and work out what each repair really cost — materials plus time. Then compare that figure to the replacement cost they already wrote down. Circle every repair that cost more than replacing it. Ask why a real repair shop would still take that job.
description.es: Repairs cost time, not just tape. Students time-stamp each of their four repairs from their report, pick an hourly rate for their own labor, and work out what each repair really cost — materials plus time. Then compare that figure to the replacement cost they already wrote down. Circle every repair that cost more than replacing it. Ask why a real repair shop would still take that job.

sayThis.en: "A toy train breaks. Glue will fix it, but it'll never be as strong. A new one is fifteen dollars, and you've got fifteen dollars. Fix it or replace it?"
sayThis.es: "A toy train breaks. Glue will fix it, but it'll never be as strong. A new one is fifteen dollars, and you've got fifteen dollars. Fix it or replace it?"

doneWhen.en: Both sides have been argued by students, not by you.
doneWhen.es: Both sides have been argued by students, not by you.

watchFor.en: The room agreeing too fast. Take the unpopular side yourself.
watchFor.es: The room agreeing too fast. Take the unpopular side yourself.

description.en: Teacher poses: "A toy train breaks. Glue will fix it but it will never be as strong. A new one costs $15. You have $15 saved. Fix or replace? Why?" Class debates. No right answer — unpack reasoning.
description.es: Teacher poses: "A toy train breaks. Glue will fix it but it will never be as strong. A new one costs $15. You have $15 saved. Fix or replace? Why?" Class debates. No right answer — unpack reasoning.

sayThis.en: "Who fixed all four? Who's got one they couldn't save? Hold it up. What would Mr. Mason say about that one?"
sayThis.es: "Who fixed all four? Who's got one they couldn't save? Hold it up. What would Mr. Mason say about that one?"

doneWhen.en: The tally is on the board and at least one student has held up an item they couldn't fix.
doneWhen.es: The tally is on the board and at least one student has held up an item they couldn't fix.

watchFor.en: Embarrassment about failures. Name your own failed repair first.
watchFor.es: Embarrassment about failures. Name your own failed repair first.

description.en: "Who fixed all 4 items successfully? Who had at least 1 they couldn't fix? What would Mr. Mason say to the items you couldn't fix?"
description.es: "Who fixed all 4 items successfully? Who had at least 1 they couldn't fix? What would Mr. Mason say to the items you couldn't fix?"

discussionQuestions: Mr. Mason said 'rushing can ruin the fix.' Did you rush any repairs? What happened?
In your repair report, what was the biggest savings — the item where fixing cost least vs. replacement cost most?
What skills did you use today? What if you could use those skills every time something breaks at home?
Mr. Mason said his grandfather's chair was still standing after decades of repairs. What's the 'chair' equivalent in your home — something old that's been fixed many times?
Is there an environmental argument for fixing vs. throwing away? What happens to things that get thrown away?
extensionIdeas: Start a class "Fix-It Log" — students record one thing they notice each week that could be fixed instead of replaced
Research the "Right to Repair" movement — why do some companies make things hard to fix?
Bring in a real small broken item (with parent permission) and brainstorm the repair approach as a class

beforeClass.en: Break the four items yourself in advance and check each one is genuinely fixable with tape, glue and paper. Decide your rate range for step 5 so the numbers stay sane.
beforeClass.es: Break the four items yourself in advance and check each one is genuinely fixable with tape, glue and paper. Decide your rate range for step 5 so the numbers stay sane.

runningLongOrShort.en: Long: cut round two to the single hardest item. Short: add a fifth item that can't be fixed at all and see what they do with it.
runningLongOrShort.es: Long: cut round two to the single hardest item. Short: add a fifth item that can't be fixed at all and see what they do with it.

description.en: Students brainstorm, categorize, and map the free or low-cost resources available to them in their school and neighborhood. Then they build a "borrow vs. buy" analysis: what needs can be met without spending money? The result is a class-built resource guide that has real utility.
description.es: Students brainstorm, categorize, and map the free or low-cost resources available to them in their school and neighborhood. Then they build a "borrow vs. buy" analysis: what needs can be met without spending money? The result is a class-built resource guide that has real utility.

20.label: 20 Minutes
20.bestFor: Tight schedules, younger students (K-1), daily scheduling
materials: Chart paper — 4 sheets, for the big community map
Library card application forms — free, teacher requests from the library in advance

description.en: "Riley and Ellis thought they needed to BUY something to stop being bored. Instead they went to the library and found everything for free. Today: what's free at OUR school?"
description.es: "Riley and Ellis thought they needed to BUY something to stop being bored. Instead they went to the library and found everything for free. Today: what's free at OUR school?"

description.en: Class shouts out things that are free at school. Teacher writes them on the board as a list. Prompt categories if needed: places (library, gym, playground), things (books, crayons, computers), services (teachers, tutoring, nurse).
description.es: Class shouts out things that are free at school. Teacher writes them on the board as a list. Prompt categories if needed: places (library, gym, playground), things (books, crayons, computers), services (teachers, tutoring, nurse).

description.en: Count the list. "We found ___ free things. Which ones could REPLACE something you'd otherwise have to buy?"
description.es: Count the list. "We found ___ free things. Which ones could REPLACE something you'd otherwise have to buy?"

description.en: "Who pays for these free things? They're not magic — someone paid for them."
description.es: "Who pays for these free things? They're not magic — someone paid for them."

discussionQuestions: If you didn't have access to school, what would it cost to get all these things elsewhere?
Ellis asked 'how can everything be free?' Miss Chen said it belongs to the community. What does that mean?
What's one thing at school you've never used that might be useful?

30.label: 30 Minutes
30.bestFor: Standard class periods, grades 1-3, weekly scheduling
materials: Chart paper — 4 sheets, for the big community map
Library card application forms — free, teacher requests from the library in advance

description.en: Students write one free/community resource per index card (at least 3 cards each). Examples: library book, park, school crayons, gym class, playground, fire station (calls are free), friend's bike, community pool. Include things you borrow from neighbors and friends.
description.es: Students write one free/community resource per index card (at least 3 cards each). Examples: library book, park, school crayons, gym class, playground, fire station (calls are free), friend's bike, community pool. Include things you borrow from neighbors and friends.

description.en: Students bring their cards to the front. Sort as a class: "Is this free, borrow-able, or must buy?" Cards go on the correct paper. Debate edge cases ("the library is free but you need a card — is it really free?")
description.es: Students bring their cards to the front. Sort as a class: "Is this free, borrow-able, or must buy?" Cards go on the correct paper. Debate edge cases ("the library is free but you need a card — is it really free?")

description.en: Together, create a simple neighborhood map on large paper: school at center, then add the free resources around it at their approximate locations (library two blocks away, park across the street, etc.). Mark each with a symbol: 📚 (library), 🌳 (park), 🏃 (recreation center), etc.
description.es: Together, create a simple neighborhood map on large paper: school at center, then add the free resources around it at their approximate locations (library two blocks away, park across the street, etc.). Mark each with a symbol: 📚 (library), 🌳 (park), 🏃 (recreation center), etc.

description.en: Count resources on the "Free/Borrow" side. "If you used these instead of buying, how much money could you save in a week? A month?"
description.es: Count resources on the "Free/Borrow" side. "If you used these instead of buying, how much money could you save in a week? A month?"

discussionQuestions: Was there anything on the 'Must Buy' list that you could BORROW instead?
Miss Chen said you can borrow craft kits from the library. Did that surprise you? What else might the library have that you didn't know about?
Why do parks and libraries exist? Who decided to make them free?
If you had a library card and used it every week, how much could you save in a year?

45.label: 45 Minutes
materials: Chart paper — 4 sheets, for the big community map
Library card application forms — free, teacher requests from the library in advance

sayThis.en: "Six categories on the board. Three minutes. Fill in as many as you can. It only counts if it's free, or almost free, to use."
sayThis.es: "Six categories on the board. Three minutes. Fill in as many as you can. It only counts if it's free, or almost free, to use."

doneWhen.en: Every category has at least two entries on the board.
doneWhen.es: Every category has at least two entries on the board.

watchFor.en: Teams stuck on the first category. Give them one example and move them on.
watchFor.es: Teams stuck on the first category. Give them one example and move them on.

description.en: Teacher writes categories on board. Teams fill in as many as they can in 3 minutes: - Learn: library, tutoring, YouTube, teacher's knowledge - Play: parks, playgrounds, community pools, school gym after hours - Create: art classes, library craft kits, school art supplies - Stay healthy: school nurse, community health events - Get food: school lunch program, community gardens, food banks - Connect: community centers, faith organizations, neighborhood apps (Buy Nothing groups)
description.es: Teacher writes categories on board. Teams fill in as many as they can in 3 minutes: - Learn: library, tutoring, YouTube, teacher's knowledge - Play: parks, playgrounds, community pools, school gym after hours - Create: art classes, library craft kits, school art supplies - Stay healthy: school nurse, community health events - Get food: school lunch program, community gardens, food banks - Connect: community centers, faith organizations, neighborhood apps (Buy Nothing groups)

sayThis.en: "Pick three. For each one — who can use it, what you get, and what it costs. And if it's free, say who's paying for it. Somebody is."
sayThis.es: "Pick three. For each one — who can use it, what you get, and what it costs. And if it's free, say who's paying for it. Somebody is."

doneWhen.en: Every student has three completed profiles.
doneWhen.es: Every student has three completed profiles.

watchFor.en: Three profiles of the same kind of place. Make them span categories.
watchFor.es: Three profiles of the same kind of place. Make them span categories.

description.en: Each student picks 3 resources from the brainstorm and completes a profile for each (using the template). They must think about: who can use it, what it provides, what it costs (if anything).
description.es: Each student picks 3 resources from the brainstorm and completes a profile for each (using the template). They must think about: who can use it, what it provides, what it costs (if anything).

sayThis.en: "Onto the map. Location, a symbol, and the saves-you line — what would you be spending if this wasn't free?"
sayThis.es: "Onto the map. Location, a symbol, and the saves-you line — what would you be spending if this wasn't free?"

doneWhen.en: Every profile is on the map with a saves-you figure.
doneWhen.es: Every profile is on the map with a saves-you figure.

watchFor.en: Crowding at the map. Send teams up one at a time and give the others a job while they wait.
watchFor.es: Crowding at the map. Send teams up one at a time and give the others a job while they wait.

description.en: Teams pool their profiles and add resources to the community map. Each resource gets a location mark, a symbol, and a "saves you ___" note (estimate how much you'd spend on this if it didn't exist for free).
description.es: Teams pool their profiles and add resources to the community map. Each resource gets a location mark, a symbol, and a "saves you ___" note (estimate how much you'd spend on this if it didn't exist for free).

steps.title: "I Didn't Know This Existed!" Sticky Notes

sayThis.en: "One or two notes. Something you found out today that you've never used but want to. They all go in this corner."
sayThis.es: "One or two notes. Something you found out today that you've never used but want to. They all go in this corner."

doneWhen.en: Every student has at least one note in the corner.
doneWhen.es: Every student has at least one note in the corner.

watchFor.en: Copying a neighbor's note. Ask what they personally want to try.
watchFor.es: Copying a neighbor's note. Ask what they personally want to try.

description.en: Students add 1-2 sticky notes to the map marking something they discovered today that they've never used but want to try. These go in a specific corner of the map.
description.es: Students add 1-2 sticky notes to the map marking something they discovered today that they've never used but want to try. These go in a specific corner of the map.

sayThis.en: "Pick the one thing on this map nobody uses enough. Ninety seconds to sell it. What it is, who it's for, what it saves you. Then the class answers one question with hands — would you actually go?"
sayThis.es: "Pick the one thing on this map nobody uses enough. Ninety seconds to sell it. What it is, who it's for, what it saves you. Then the class answers one question with hands — would you actually go?"

doneWhen.en: Every team has pitched and every score is tallied on the board.
doneWhen.es: Every team has pitched and every score is tallied on the board.

watchFor.en: Pitches that describe instead of persuade. Remind them the question is would you go, not what is it.
watchFor.es: Pitches that describe instead of persuade. Remind them the question is would you go, not what is it.

description.en: Each team picks the one resource on the map they think is most underused and gets ninety seconds to sell it to the class — what it is, who it is for, what it saves you. The class scores each pitch by show of hands on one question only: would you actually go? Tally the scores on the board. Ask what made the winning pitch work, and why good things stay unused when nobody talks about them.
description.es: Each team picks the one resource on the map they think is most underused and gets ninety seconds to sell it to the class — what it is, who it is for, what it saves you. The class scores each pitch by show of hands on one question only: would you actually go? Tally the scores on the board. Ask what made the winning pitch work, and why good things stay unused when nobody talks about them.

sayThis.en: "Monday to Friday, using only what's on this map, spending nothing. Plan one family's week."
sayThis.es: "Monday to Friday, using only what's on this map, spending nothing. Plan one family's week."

doneWhen.en: One complete week has been presented to the class.
doneWhen.es: One complete week has been presented to the class.

watchFor.en: Five days of the same thing. Push for variety across the categories.
watchFor.es: Five days of the same thing. Push for variety across the categories.

description.en: As a class, design a hypothetical "Week of Free Activities" using only resources on the map. What would you do Monday through Friday that costs $0? Present one family's week.
description.es: As a class, design a hypothetical "Week of Free Activities" using only resources on the map. What would you do Monday through Friday that costs $0? Present one family's week.

discussionQuestions: The library uses tax money. You and your family already paid for it — are you getting your money's worth?
Ellis said 'how can everything be free?' Is it actually free, or is the cost hidden? Who pays and how?
What's the most valuable free resource in our neighborhood that most people don't use?
Could you live an entire month using only free community resources for entertainment and learning? What would you miss?
Mr. Mason says 'the best things in life are free.' Is that true? What's the limit of that idea?
extensionIdeas: Visit the local library and get library cards for anyone who doesn't have one
Assign: "Resource Hunt" — find one free or borrowable resource at home you've never used and report back
Research: what's in the "Library of Things" at your nearest library? (Many lend tools, instruments, games, even seeds!)

beforeClass.en: Write the six categories on the board before the lesson. Have two local examples ready for each; the brainstorm dies without seeds. Put the class map up where four teams can reach it at once.
beforeClass.es: Write the six categories on the board before the lesson. Have two local examples ready for each; the brainstorm dies without seeds. Put the class map up where four teams can reach it at once.

runningLongOrShort.en: Long: cut the sticky-note step and fold it into the pitch. Short: add a round where each team must find a resource nobody else listed.
runningLongOrShort.es: Long: cut the sticky-note step and fold it into the pitch. Short: add a round where each team must find a resource nobody else listed.

focus: Name one free thing in your school or town
Add it to the class map (draw it)
Tell who can use it

List and group free or low-cost resources
Mark them on a community map
Decide one need you can meet without money

Categorize resources and map them with a key
Build a borrow-vs-buy comparison

description.en: Students start with equal small "investments" (tokens or paper shapes). Through structured giving rounds, they observe what happens to the group's total when people share freely. The simulation generates the experience Frances describes — giving doesn't deplete you; it generates reciprocal giving and collective abundance.
description.es: Students start with equal small "investments" (tokens or paper shapes). Through structured giving rounds, they observe what happens to the group's total when people share freely. The simulation generates the experience Frances describes — giving doesn't deplete you; it generates reciprocal giving and collective abundance.

20.label: 20 Minutes
20.bestFor: Tight schedules, younger students (K-1), daily scheduling
materials: Construction paper — 30 sheets, three colors for three token values
Plain paper — 40 sheets, for the investment journal
Small envelopes — 20, for holding tokens (or fold paper pockets, free)

description.en: "The friends grew more vegetables than they could use. They gave them away. In return, neighbors gave them jam, cookies, and flowers. Today we're going to see what happens when everyone shares." Distribute 3 tokens per student.
description.es: "The friends grew more vegetables than they could use. They gave them away. In return, neighbors gave them jam, cookies, and flowers. Today we're going to see what happens when everyone shares." Distribute 3 tokens per student.

description.en: "Give ONE token to someone you think needs it or would appreciate it. You choose who. You may give to anyone in the room." Observe: every student gives one and (likely) receives one or more.
description.es: "Give ONE token to someone you think needs it or would appreciate it. You choose who. You may give to anyone in the room." Observe: every student gives one and (likely) receives one or more.

description.en: "Count your tokens. Did you end up with more, less, or the same as you started?" Class show of hands: more / same / fewer. Tally.
description.es: "Count your tokens. Did you end up with more, less, or the same as you started?" Class show of hands: more / same / fewer. Tally.

description.en: "What happened? Did giving away one token leave you with less? Why or why not?"
description.es: "What happened? Did giving away one token leave you with less? Why or why not?"

discussionQuestions: Frances said there's always enough when we share. Did today show that?
Did anyone give more than one token? Did they end up with less?
What if nobody gave any tokens — would that be better?

30.label: 30 Minutes
30.bestFor: Standard class periods, grades 1-3, weekly scheduling
materials: Construction paper — 30 sheets, three colors for three token values
Plain paper — 40 sheets, for the investment journal
Small envelopes — 20, for holding tokens (or fold paper pockets, free)

description.en: Distribute 5 tokens. Students write "5" in the START row of their journal.
description.es: Distribute 5 tokens. Students write "5" in the START row of their journal.

description.en: "Give however many tokens you want to whoever you want. You don't have to give any. You don't have to give equally." After round: count tokens, record in journal row.
description.es: "Give however many tokens you want to whoever you want. You don't have to give any. You don't have to give equally." After round: count tokens, record in journal row.

description.en: "Frances grew more than she could use — she gave the excess. This round: give away any tokens you have above 3. Keep 3 for yourself, share the rest." After round: count and record.
description.es: "Frances grew more than she could use — she gave the excess. This round: give away any tokens you have above 3. Keep 3 for yourself, share the rest." After round: count and record.

description.en: Teacher tallies: how many tokens does the class have total? Did the total go up, down, or stay the same? (It stays the same — conservation of tokens. Point this out. The distribution changed, not the total.)
description.es: Teacher tallies: how many tokens does the class have total? Did the total go up, down, or stay the same? (It stays the same — conservation of tokens. Point this out. The distribution changed, not the total.)

description.en: "What changed between Round 1 and Round 2? What does it mean to share only the 'excess'? Frances had 3 full baskets — more than enough. That's why sharing felt easy."
description.es: "What changed between Round 1 and Round 2? What does it mean to share only the 'excess'? Frances had 3 full baskets — more than enough. That's why sharing felt easy."

discussionQuestions: Why is it easier to share when you have MORE than enough?
Frances said 'sharing creates abundance.' What does that mean if the total number of tokens didn't change?
What's the difference between giving because you have extra vs. giving when you're barely getting by?
The seeds the friends planted in Frances's garden (Chapter 2) grew into enough to share. What was the 'investment' that made that possible?

45.label: 45 Minutes
materials: Construction paper — 30 sheets, three colors for three token values
Plain paper — 40 sheets, for the investment journal
Small envelopes — 20, for holding tokens (or fold paper pockets, free)

sayThis.en: "Back to chapter two. Riley planted seeds and got a whole garden. What did she put in? What came back? Today we do the same thing with tokens."
sayThis.es: "Back to chapter two. Riley planted seeds and got a whole garden. What did she put in? What came back? Today we do the same thing with tokens."

doneWhen.en: Every card names one thing invested and one thing returned.
doneWhen.es: Every card names one thing invested and one thing returned.

watchFor.en: Answers only about flowers. Push toward time and patience as the investment.
watchFor.es: Answers only about flowers. Push toward time and patience as the investment.

description.en: Students complete their Investment Card. "Think back to Chapter 2. Riley planted flower seeds. The return was a whole garden. What did she invest? What did she get back?" Then: "Today's simulation shows the same cycle with tokens."
description.es: Students complete their Investment Card. "Think back to Chapter 2. Riley planted flower seeds. The return was a whole garden. What did she invest? What did she get back?" Then: "Today's simulation shows the same cycle with tokens."

sayThis.en: "Here are your tokens." Nothing else. Don't explain the amounts.
sayThis.es: "Here are your tokens." Nothing else. Don't explain the amounts.

doneWhen.en: Every student has their envelope and at least one person has said "that's not fair".
doneWhen.es: Every student has their envelope and at least one person has said "that's not fair".

watchFor.en: The moment someone notices. Let it happen. Don't answer the question yet.
watchFor.es: The moment someone notices. Let it happen. Don't answer the question yet.

description.en: Distribute 10 tokens unevenly: some students get 15 (the "abundant harvest" students), some get 8, some get 5, some get 3 (the "scarce" students). Do NOT announce this is unequal — let them discover.
description.es: Distribute 10 tokens unevenly: some students get 15 (the "abundant harvest" students), some get 8, some get 5, some get 3 (the "scarce" students). Do NOT announce this is unequal — let them discover.

sayThis.en: "Give to whoever you want, as much as you want. No rules at all. Write down every give in your journal."
sayThis.es: "Give to whoever you want, as much as you want. No rules at all. Write down every give in your journal."

doneWhen.en: Every journal has at least one entry, including "gave nothing".
doneWhen.es: Every journal has at least one entry, including "gave nothing".

watchFor.en: Who gives and who gets ignored. Note two names — you'll use them in the last step.
watchFor.es: Who gives and who gets ignored. Note two names — you'll use them in the last step.

description.en: Open giving round. "Give however you want to whoever you want. No rules." Record in journal. Observe who gives, who receives, whether inequity narrows or widens.
description.es: Open giving round. "Give however you want to whoever you want. No rules." Record in journal. Observe who gives, who receives, whether inequity narrows or widens.

sayThis.en: "New rule. Five tokens is what a person needs. Anything over five is extra, and the extra gets shared first."
sayThis.es: "New rule. Five tokens is what a person needs. Anything over five is extra, and the extra gets shared first."

doneWhen.en: Every student has written their new total in their journal.
doneWhen.es: Every student has written their new total in their journal.

watchFor.en: Hoarders hiding tokens. Don't police it — record it. It's data.
watchFor.es: Hoarders hiding tokens. Don't police it — record it. It's data.

description.en: "This round: everyone identifies their 'need' (a baseline of 5 tokens). Anyone with more than 5 shares the excess first." Record. Does inequity narrow?
description.es: "This round: everyone identifies their 'need' (a baseline of 5 tokens). Anyone with more than 5 shares the excess first." Record. Does inequity narrow?

sayThis.en: "Last rule. If somebody gives to you, you have to give to somebody. Doesn't have to be back to them. Watch what happens to the room."
sayThis.es: "Last rule. If somebody gives to you, you have to give to somebody. Doesn't have to be back to them. Watch what happens to the room."

doneWhen.en: At least one chain of three is drawn on the board.
doneWhen.es: At least one chain of three is drawn on the board.

watchFor.en: Chains forming. Point one out loud as it happens.
watchFor.es: Chains forming. Point one out loud as it happens.

description.en: "This round: if someone gives to you, you must give something back — not necessarily to them, but to someone." Record. Observe the chain-reaction effect.
description.es: "This round: if someone gives to you, you must give something back — not necessarily to them, but to someone." Record. Observe the chain-reaction effect.

sayThis.en: "Three columns. After each round, the highest number in the room and the lowest. Subtract. That's the gap. Copy the three numbers down and draw the line."
sayThis.es: "Three columns. After each round, the highest number in the room and the lowest. Subtract. That's the gap. Copy the three numbers down and draw the line."

doneWhen.en: Every student has drawn the line and the winning rule is circled on the board.
doneWhen.es: Every student has drawn the line and the winning rule is circled on the board.

watchFor.en: Students reading a falling line as everyone getting poorer. Ask what happened to the class total.
watchFor.es: Students reading a falling line as everyone getting poorer. Ask what happened to the class total.

description.en: Three columns on the board: after Round 1, after Round 2, after Round 3. For each, record the highest token count in the room and the lowest, and subtract to get the gap. Students copy the three numbers and draw the line on scrap paper. The shape of that line is the whole lesson. Ask which rule closed the gap fastest, whether closing it made the room better off in total, and what happened to the people who started with the most.
description.es: Three columns on the board: after Round 1, after Round 2, after Round 3. For each, record the highest token count in the room and the lowest, and subtract to get the gap. Students copy the three numbers and draw the line on scrap paper. The shape of that line is the whole lesson. Ask which rule closed the gap fastest, whether closing it made the room better off in total, and what happened to the people who started with the most.

sayThis.en: "Which round felt best? Not which was fairest — which felt best. Were they the same round? And what happened to the people who started with the most?"
sayThis.es: "Which round felt best? Not which was fairest — which felt best. Were they the same round? And what happened to the people who started with the most?"

doneWhen.en: Both questions have been answered and the low-start students have spoken.

watchFor.en: The students who started with three. Ask them directly, last.
watchFor.es: The students who started with three. Ask them directly, last.

description.en: Compare all three rounds. "Which round felt best? Which reduced the gap between the most and least token-holders? Why?"
description.es: Compare all three rounds. "Which round felt best? Which reduced the gap between the most and least token-holders? Why?"

discussionQuestions: In Round 1, did the gap between the richest and poorest students get bigger or smaller? What about Round 3?
Frances grew seeds into food. The seeds cost nothing and came from nature. But the investment of TIME changed everything. What does that tell us?
Layla gave away vegetables. Neighbors gave back jam and cookies and flowers. Did Layla end up poorer?
Benny asked 'to who?' when they decided to share. How do you decide who to give to when you have extra?
The class as a whole had the same number of tokens the whole time. So what did 'abundance' actually mean?
extensionIdeas: Connect to real-world abundance: research community gardens, food banks, mutual aid networks — organizations built on the idea that sharing excess creates community resilience
Write Frances's speech from the episode: "You learned about investment and patience" — expand it into a 3-paragraph essay from the perspective of one of the friends

description.en: Each student writes $50 on a budget card as their starting balance - Display all 10 items so students can plan - Explain bidding: "Start at $5. You can bid higher. Highest bidder wins." - Introduce budget tracking sheet: record each purchase
description.es: Each student writes $50 on a budget card as their starting balance - Display all 10 items so students can plan - Explain bidding: "Start at $5. You can bid higher. Highest bidder wins." - Introduce budget tracking sheet: record each purchase

description.en: Auction 5 items - After each sale, pause: "How much money do you have left?" - Students record purchases on tracking sheet
description.es: Auction 5 items - After each sale, pause: "How much money do you have left?" - Students record purchases on tracking sheet

description.en: "What have you noticed? What's your strategy for the remaining items?"
description.es: "What have you noticed? What's your strategy for the remaining items?"

description.en: Auction final 5 items (include some "surprise" items - mystery bags) - Watch for strategic behavior: saving vs. spending
description.es: Auction final 5 items (include some "surprise" items - mystery bags) - Watch for strategic behavior: saving vs. spending

description.en: Count: Who spent all money? Who saved some? - Discuss: Which items went for highest prices? Why? - Graph: Actual sale prices vs. teacher's guess
description.es: Count: Who spent all money? Who saved some? - Discuss: Which items went for highest prices? Why? - Graph: Actual sale prices vs. teacher's guess

discussionQuestions: What was your strategy?
Did you run out of money before getting something you wanted?
What would you do differently next time?
How did competition affect prices?
extensionIdeas: Students calculate "satisfaction rating" for purchases - did high-priced items make them happier?

45.label: 45 Minutes
materials: 15+ auction items (variety: highly desirable, medium, and less popular)
Budget card for each student — they write $100 as the starting balance and subtract each winning bid
Auction catalog (list of all items with descriptions)

description.en: Students write $100 on their budget card and take an auction catalog - Students review all items and plan strategy - Budget worksheet: rank items by desire, set maximum bid for each - Discuss: opportunity cost ("If you spend $40 on Item 1, what can't you buy?") - Introduce roles: some students will be bidders, others will be auctioneer's assistants (tracking prices)
description.es: Students write $100 on their budget card and take an auction catalog - Students review all items and plan strategy - Budget worksheet: rank items by desire, set maximum bid for each - Discuss: opportunity cost ("If you spend $40 on Item 1, what can't you buy?") - Introduce roles: some students will be bidders, others will be auctioneer's assistants (tracking prices)

description.en: Auction first 5 items - Teacher as auctioneer: "Do I hear $5? $10? Going once, going twice, SOLD to bidder #7!" - Assistants record winning bids on chart - After each sale, brief pause for students to update budgets
description.es: Auction first 5 items - Teacher as auctioneer: "Do I hear $5? $10? Going once, going twice, SOLD to bidder #7!" - Assistants record winning bids on chart - After each sale, brief pause for students to update budgets

description.en: Chart first 5 prices - Discuss: "What patterns do you see? Which items went high? Why?" - "How many of you are running low on money?" - Introduce concepts: bidding war, market value, reserve price
description.es: Chart first 5 prices - Discuss: "What patterns do you see? Which items went high? Why?" - "How many of you are running low on money?" - Introduce concepts: bidding war, market value, reserve price

description.en: Include 3 mystery bags/boxes (unknown contents) - Students must bid blind - Discuss: "How do you decide value when you don't know what's inside?" - Unwrap after bidding - discuss willingness to take risks
description.es: Include 3 mystery bags/boxes (unknown contents) - Students must bid blind - Discuss: "How do you decide value when you don't know what's inside?" - Unwrap after bidding - discuss willingness to take risks

description.en: Volunteer students take over as auctioneers - Final items auctioned - Observe strategic behavior: desperation bidding, saving, bargain hunting
description.es: Volunteer students take over as auctioneers - Final items auctioned - Observe strategic behavior: desperation bidding, saving, bargain hunting

description.en: Create bar graph: all items and their final prices - Calculate: average price, highest price, lowest price - Discuss findings: - "Did expensive items make people happier?" - "What determined final price: actual value or how much people wanted it?" - "What's the difference between what something costs and what it's worth?" - "Who managed their budget best? How?"
description.es: Create bar graph: all items and their final prices - Calculate: average price, highest price, lowest price - Discuss findings: - "Did expensive items make people happier?" - "What determined final price: actual value or how much people wanted it?" - "What's the difference between what something costs and what it's worth?" - "Who managed their budget best? How?"

discussionQuestions: What was your bidding strategy? Did it work?
