title.en: Baker's Math: Recipe Costs & Bakery Economics
title.es: Baker's Math: Recipe Costs & Bakery Economics

20.label: 20 Minutes
20.bestFor: Tight schedules, younger students (K-1), daily scheduling
20.activityName: Paper Pastry with Quick Cost Tracking
materials: Four parts laid out in trays — bases, frosting layers, wrappers, toppers
A large poster with the four part prices on it
One paper plate per student to build on

description.en: Show the four parts. Point to the price poster: "A base costs 25¢. A frosting layer costs 50¢. A wrapper costs 25¢. A topper costs 75¢."
description.es: Show the four parts. Point to the price poster: "A base costs 25¢. A frosting layer costs 50¢. A wrapper costs 25¢. A topper costs 75¢."

description.en: Each student takes one of each part, glues them together on their plate, and writes their name on the wrapper.
description.es: Each student takes one of each part, glues them together on their plate, and writes their name on the wrapper.

description.en: Write on the board: 25¢ + 50¢ + 25¢ + 75¢. Students help count: "What's 25 plus 50? Now add 25 more..." Total: $1.75
description.es: Write on the board: 25¢ + 50¢ + 25¢ + 75¢. Students help count: "What's 25 plus 50? Now add 25 more..." Total: $1.75

description.en: "Our pastry costs $1.75 to make. Should we sell it for $1.75?" (No, no profit!) "How about $2.00? $2.50? $3.00?"
description.es: "Our pastry costs $1.75 to make. Should we sell it for $1.75?" (No, no profit!) "How about $2.00? $2.50? $3.00?"

discussionQuestions: How much did our trail mix cost to make?
Would you buy it for $2.00?
Why do we need to charge MORE than it costs to make?
What could a bakery do with the extra money? (Pay workers, buy more ingredients, keep lights on)

30.label: 30 Minutes
30.bestFor: Standard class periods, grades 1-3, weekly scheduling
materials: Cost tracking worksheet, one per student or group
Small bags or folded paper boxes for packaging
A price comparison card showing what a party shop charges for a paper cake topper

description.en: Display the build recipe on the board with what each part costs in bulk. Example: "Cardstock $2.00 (we need 4 sheets), Tissue paper $1.50 (we need 1 pack), Tape 50¢ (we need 2 feet)"
description.es: Display the build recipe on the board with what each part costs in bulk. Example: "Cardstock $2.00 (we need 4 sheets), Tissue paper $1.50 (we need 1 pack), Tape 50¢ (we need 2 feet)"

description.en: Groups measure, cut and assemble following the recipe. One student is the parts tracker, marking off every piece used — including the ones cut wrong.
description.es: Groups measure, cut and assemble following the recipe. One student is the parts tracker, marking off every piece used — including the ones cut wrong.

description.en: Fill out the cost worksheet: list each part and its cost - Add all costs together to find TOTAL COST - Count the number of pastries finished - Divide total cost by pastries: COST PER ITEM
description.es: Fill out the cost worksheet: list each part and its cost - Add all costs together to find TOTAL COST - Count the number of pastries finished - Divide total cost by pastries: COST PER ITEM

description.en: Groups decide a selling price. It has to be higher than the cost per item. Compare to the shop card: "A paper cake topper at the party shop costs $1.50. Ours costs 40¢ to make. What should we charge?"
description.es: Groups decide a selling price. It has to be higher than the cost per item. Compare to the shop card: "A paper cake topper at the party shop costs $1.50. Ours costs 40¢ to make. What should we charge?"

description.en: Share prices across the class. Discuss: "Why are prices different? Which would make the most profit? Who wasted the most cardstock?"
description.es: Share prices across the class. Discuss: "Why are prices different? Which would make the most profit? Who wasted the most cardstock?"

discussionQuestions: What was our total cost for all ingredients?
How many servings did we make?
What's the cost for ONE serving?
How much should we charge to make a profit?
Is our price fair compared to the store price?
What happens if we charge less than it costs to make?
extensionIdeas: Create price tags and packaging labels for finished product

45.label: 45 Minutes
materials: Cardstock, tissue paper, colored paper and tape
Bakery branding materials (markers, cardstock for signs)
Shop comparison cards showing party-store prices for similar paper pieces

description.en: Teams choose a build from 2-3 options (a simple cupcake, a layered cake slice, a decorated cookie shape) - Receive the parts cost sheet - Predict: "How much will this cost to make? How much should we charge?" - Assign roles: Head Baker, Parts Manager, Cost Tracker, Packaging Designer
description.es: Teams choose a build from 2-3 options (a simple cupcake, a layered cake slice, a decorated cookie shape) - Receive the parts cost sheet - Predict: "How much will this cost to make? How much should we charge?" - Assign roles: Head Baker, Parts Manager, Cost Tracker, Packaging Designer

description.en: Follow the build recipe, measuring and cutting each part - Parts Manager tracks the ACTUAL pieces used, mis-cuts included (waste costs money!) - Note any mistakes or extra parts needed - Package the finished pastries attractively
description.es: Follow the build recipe, measuring and cutting each part - Parts Manager tracks the ACTUAL pieces used, mis-cuts included (waste costs money!) - Note any mistakes or extra parts needed - Package the finished pastries attractively

description.en: Calculate parts costs (actual pieces used, not just the ones that worked) - Add packaging costs (bags: 10¢ each, labels: 5¢ each, ribbon: 3¢ each) - Add "labor cost" (optional advanced concept): "If each team member earned $5/hour and you worked 20 minutes, that's $1.67 in labor" - Calculate cost PER ITEM (total cost ÷ number of pastries made) - Document all calculations on the worksheet
description.es: Calculate parts costs (actual pieces used, not just the ones that worked) - Add packaging costs (bags: 10¢ each, labels: 5¢ each, ribbon: 3¢ each) - Add "labor cost" (optional advanced concept): "If each team member earned $5/hour and you worked 20 minutes, that's $1.67 in labor" - Calculate cost PER ITEM (total cost ÷ number of pastries made) - Document all calculations on the worksheet

description.en: Research: display the party-shop prices for similar paper pieces - Set a price that covers ALL costs plus the profit you want - Write the justification: "We charge $2.50 because it costs $1.20 to make and we want $1.30 profit per item" - Design price tags showing the price and why it is worth it - Create a bakery name and logo for the labels
description.es: Research: display the party-shop prices for similar paper pieces - Set a price that covers ALL costs plus the profit you want - Write the justification: "We charge $2.50 because it costs $1.20 to make and we want $1.30 profit per item" - Design price tags showing the price and why it is worth it - Create a bakery name and logo for the labels

description.en: Calculate: if you sold every pastry at your price, what is the total revenue? - Subtract total cost = TOTAL PROFIT - Discuss: "Is this a sustainable business?" - Compare prices across teams: "Why are prices different?" - "What could you do with the profit?" (Reinvest, pay yourself, expand the bakery)
description.es: Calculate: if you sold every pastry at your price, what is the total revenue? - Subtract total cost = TOTAL PROFIT - Discuss: "Is this a sustainable business?" - Compare prices across teams: "Why are prices different?" - "What could you do with the profit?" (Reinvest, pay yourself, expand the bakery)

discussionQuestions: What surprised you about the costs?
Was any ingredient more expensive than you expected?
How much profit should a business make—a little or a lot? Why?
What happens if you price too low? Too high?
Why do real bakeries charge different prices for different items?
Besides ingredients, what OTHER costs does a real bakery have? (Rent, electricity, wages, equipment)
How does knowing exact costs help you run a business?
Could your family run a bakery business with what you learned today?
extensionIdeas: Actually "sell" to another class using paper-clip coins, track real profit
Compare costs of making vs. buying (make a batch vs. buy from store)
Research local bakery pricing and cost structures
Design complete business plan including monthly costs and revenue projections
Calculate break-even point (how many items must you sell to cover costs?)

title.en: The Morning Market: Fresh or Not?
title.es: The Morning Market: Fresh or Not?

20.label: 20 Minutes
20.bestFor: Tight schedules, younger students (K-1), daily scheduling
20.activityName: Fresh or Not? The Perishable Challenge
materials: * - 10-15 picture cards showing various items (food and non-food)
Two sorting areas (circles on floor or desk sections)

description.en: Show students a banana: "Fresh today, brown tomorrow—why?". Explain some things last, others don't. Introduce sorting challenge
description.es: Show students a banana: "Fresh today, brown tomorrow—why?". Explain some things last, others don't. Introduce sorting challenge

description.en: Students take turns selecting a card. Place in correct category: Spoils Fast or Lasts Long. Class votes if unsure. Discuss each placement
description.es: Students take turns selecting a card. Place in correct category: Spoils Fast or Lasts Long. Class votes if unsure. Discuss each placement

description.en: Teacher calls out items. Students point to correct category. Speed increases for challenge
description.es: Teacher calls out items. Students point to correct category. Speed increases for challenge

description.en: "Would you sell fish today or save for tomorrow? Why?". "What happens if you wait to sell milk?". Connect to morning market story Items to Include:. Spoils Fast: fish, milk, bread, lettuce, bananas, strawberries. Lasts Long: toys, books, clothes, pencils, rocks, jewelry
description.es: "Would you sell fish today or save for tomorrow? Why?". "What happens if you wait to sell milk?". Connect to morning market story Items to Include:. Spoils Fast: fish, milk, bread, lettuce, bananas, strawberries. Lasts Long: toys, books, clothes, pencils, rocks, jewelry

discussionQuestions: Would you sell fish today or save for tomorrow? Why?
What happens if you wait to sell milk?

30.label: 30 Minutes
30.bestFor: Standard class periods, grades 1-3, weekly scheduling
30.activityName: Fresh or Not? The Perishable Challenge
materials: Item cards (3 per student: 1 perishable, 2 non-perishable)
Price chart showing rounds and values
Scrap-paper budget card per student ($20 written at the top, crossed out and rewritten as it is spent)

description.en: Each student receives: * 1 perishable card (fish, bread, milk, fruit) * 2 non-perishable cards (toys, books, tools, clothes). Explain three trading rounds. Show price chart on board
description.es: Each student receives: * 1 perishable card (fish, bread, milk, fruit) * 2 non-perishable cards (toys, books, tools, clothes). Explain three trading rounds. Show price chart on board

description.en: Timer set for 3 minutes. Prices: Perishables $10, Non-perishables $5. Students can sell to "market buyer" (teacher/volunteer). Buyers walk around making offers. Record what each student sells
description.es: Timer set for 3 minutes. Prices: Perishables $10, Non-perishables $5. Students can sell to "market buyer" (teacher/volunteer). Buyers walk around making offers. Record what each student sells

description.en: Timer set for 2 minutes. Prices: Perishables DROP to $5, Non-perishables stay $5. Students who held perishables see value decrease. More selling happens. Visual: Update price chart dramatically
description.es: Timer set for 2 minutes. Prices: Perishables DROP to $5, Non-perishables stay $5. Students who held perishables see value decrease. More selling happens. Visual: Update price chart dramatically

description.en: Timer set for 1 minute. Prices: Perishables DROP to $1, Non-perishables stay $5. Last chance to sell. Those who held perishables feel real impact
description.es: Timer set for 1 minute. Prices: Perishables DROP to $1, Non-perishables stay $5. Last chance to sell. Those who held perishables feel real impact

description.en: Students count final money. Graph results on board. Who made the most? What strategy did they use?. Who sold perishables early? Late?
description.es: Students count final money. Graph results on board. Who made the most? What strategy did they use?. Who sold perishables early? Late?

discussionQuestions: Who sold fish in Round 1? Why?
Who waited? How did that work out?
What would you do differently next time?
Why don't toy prices drop like fish prices?

45.label: 45 Minutes
45.activityName: Fresh or Not? The Perishable Challenge
materials: Mixed inventory cards (10 items per student: 4 perishable, 6 non-perishable)
Scrap-paper budget card per student ($50 written at the top, crossed out and rewritten as it is spent)

description.en: Students set up stalls with inventory. Receive starting cash $50. Review price tracking sheet. Assign initial "buyers" (rotating role). Practice using tracking sheet
description.es: Students set up stalls with inventory. Receive starting cash $50. Review price tracking sheet. Assign initial "buyers" (rotating role). Practice using tracking sheet

description.en: Timer: 5 minutes of active trading. Starting prices: * Perishables: $8 each (fish, fruit, milk, bread) * Non-perishables: $5 each (toys, books, tools, clothes, crafts, jewelry). Buyers visit stalls, negotiate, purchase. Sellers mark sales on tracking sheet. Rotate buyer badges after 3 minutes
description.es: Timer: 5 minutes of active trading. Starting prices: * Perishables: $8 each (fish, fruit, milk, bread) * Non-perishables: $5 each (toys, books, tools, clothes, crafts, jewelry). Buyers visit stalls, negotiate, purchase. Sellers mark sales on tracking sheet. Rotate buyer badges after 3 minutes

description.en: Timer: 4 minutes of active trading. Price changes announced dramatically: * Perishables: DROP to $4 each * Non-perishables: STAY $5 each. Discussion pause: "Notice anything about your fish value?". Continue trading. Sellers see depreciation impact. Rotate buyers again
description.es: Timer: 4 minutes of active trading. Price changes announced dramatically: * Perishables: DROP to $4 each * Non-perishables: STAY $5 each. Discussion pause: "Notice anything about your fish value?". Continue trading. Sellers see depreciation impact. Rotate buyers again

description.en: Timer: 3 minutes of active trading. Final price changes: * Perishables: DROP to $2 each * Non-perishables: STAY $5 each. Urgent selling begins. Some students stuck with near-worthless perishables. Close market
description.es: Timer: 3 minutes of active trading. Final price changes: * Perishables: DROP to $2 each * Non-perishables: STAY $5 each. Urgent selling begins. Some students stuck with near-worthless perishables. Close market

description.en: Students calculate total revenue. Create bar graphs showing: * Starting inventory value * Final revenue * Difference (profit/loss). Class data: graph average revenue by strategy. Identify patterns: early sellers vs. holders Price Tracking Sheet Format: ``` Name: ________________ Stall #: ____ INVENTORY: Perishables: [ ] Fish [ ] Fruit [ ] Milk [ ] Bread Non-perishables: [ ] Toy [ ] Book [ ] Tool [ ] Clothes [ ] Craft [ ] Jewelry PERIOD 1 (Perish=$8, Non-perish=$5): Sold: ____________ Revenue: $______ PERIOD 2 (Perish=$4, Non-perish=$5): Sold: ____________ Revenue: $______ PERIOD 3 (Perish=$2, Non-perish=$5): Sold: ____________ Revenue: $______ TOTAL REVENUE: $______ Starting inventory value: $______ Profit/Loss: $______ ```
description.es: Students calculate total revenue. Create bar graphs showing: * Starting inventory value * Final revenue * Difference (profit/loss). Class data: graph average revenue by strategy. Identify patterns: early sellers vs. holders Price Tracking Sheet Format: ``` Name: ________________ Stall #: ____ INVENTORY: Perishables: [ ] Fish [ ] Fruit [ ] Milk [ ] Bread Non-perishables: [ ] Toy [ ] Book [ ] Tool [ ] Clothes [ ] Craft [ ] Jewelry PERIOD 1 (Perish=$8, Non-perish=$5): Sold: ____________ Revenue: $______ PERIOD 2 (Perish=$4, Non-perish=$5): Sold: ____________ Revenue: $______ PERIOD 3 (Perish=$2, Non-perish=$5): Sold: ____________ Revenue: $______ TOTAL REVENUE: $______ Starting inventory value: $______ Profit/Loss: $______ ```

discussionQuestions: What strategy worked best? Why?
Who sold all perishables in Period 1? How did that turn out?
Who held onto fish until Period 3? What happened?
Would you change your strategy if we played again?

description.es: Groups discuss: "Should we each make our own tiny garden, or pool our money for one big garden?". Calculate: * Individual: $20 buys very little * Pooled: $80-100 buys full garden with all supplies. Make group decision (guided toward pooling for lesson)

description.en: Groups draw garden on poster paper. Divide into plots (one per student). Add paths, shared tool area, water source. Select seeds/plants from catalog. Glue pictures in each plot
description.es: Groups draw garden on poster paper. Divide into plots (one per student). Add paths, shared tool area, water source. Select seeds/plants from catalog. Glue pictures in each plot

description.en: Decide: "If tomatoes grow in one plot, does only that person get them?". Discuss fair sharing since everyone contributed. Record sharing agreement
description.es: Decide: "If tomatoes grow in one plot, does only that person get them?". Discuss fair sharing since everyone contributed. Record sharing agreement

description.en: Each group shows garden design. Shares one thing about their sharing plan
description.es: Each group shows garden design. Shares one thing about their sharing plan

discussionQuestions: Why did pooling money help more than individual spending?
How should you share the vegetables when they grow?
What if someone contributed seeds instead of money—should they still get vegetables?

45.label: 45 Minutes
materials: Large grid paper or poster board (one per group)
Scrap-paper budget card per student ($30 written at the top, crossed out and rewritten as it is spent)
Resource cards (seeds, tools, soil, water access, time/labor)
Seed catalog or printed plant images
Measuring tools (rulers, tape measures for scale)

description.en: Present community garden challenge: * Neighborhood has empty lot (12' x 16' = 192 sq ft) * Could become community garden if neighbors invest. Show cost breakdown: * Fence: $50 * Soil (all plots): $40 * Seeds: $30 * Shared tools: $30 * Water hookup: $50 * Total needed: $200. Class has combined $180 in cash (6 students × $30). Gap: $20—someone needs to contribute non-monetary resources
description.es: Present community garden challenge: * Neighborhood has empty lot (12' x 16' = 192 sq ft) * Could become community garden if neighbors invest. Show cost breakdown: * Fence: $50 * Soil (all plots): $40 * Seeds: $30 * Shared tools: $30 * Water hookup: $50 * Total needed: $200. Class has combined $180 in cash (6 students × $30). Gap: $20—someone needs to contribute non-monetary resources

description.en: Students receive varied resources: * 4 students: $30 cash each * 1 student: $20 cash + seed packets (worth $10) * 1 student: $10 cash + tools to share (worth $20). Complete contribution worksheet: * Name * Cash contributed: $_____ * Non-cash contributed: _____ * Total value: $_____. Pool all resources in center table. Calculate if goal met ($200 total)
description.es: Students receive varied resources: * 4 students: $30 cash each * 1 student: $20 cash + seed packets (worth $10) * 1 student: $10 cash + tools to share (worth $20). Complete contribution worksheet: * Name * Cash contributed: $_____ * Non-cash contributed: _____ * Total value: $_____. Pool all resources in center table. Calculate if goal met ($200 total)

description.en: Groups (6-8 students) design garden layout: * Use grid paper (each square = 2 sq ft) * Divide into individual plots (4-6 sq ft per person) * Include shared spaces:. Tool shed area. Compost bin. Pathways. Water access point. Assign plots fairly: * Option A: Equal sizes for all * Option B: Larger plots for larger investors * Group decides which is "fair". Select plants for each plot from catalog. Label everything clearly
description.es: Groups (6-8 students) design garden layout: * Use grid paper (each square = 2 sq ft) * Divide into individual plots (4-6 sq ft per person) * Include shared spaces:. Tool shed area. Compost bin. Pathways. Water access point. Assign plots fairly: * Option A: Equal sizes for all * Option B: Larger plots for larger investors * Group decides which is "fair". Select plants for each plot from catalog. Label everything clearly

description.en: Use provided data for expected harvest: * Tomatoes: 20 lbs per plot * Lettuce: 10 heads per plot * Carrots: 15 bunches per plot. Students calculate: * Their investment: $______ * Their expected harvest value (at market price): $______ * ROI: (Harvest value. Investment) ÷ Investment. Example: Invested $30, harvest worth $60 → ROI = 100% (doubled money)
description.es: Use provided data for expected harvest: * Tomatoes: 20 lbs per plot * Lettuce: 10 heads per plot * Carrots: 15 bunches per plot. Students calculate: * Their investment: $______ * Their expected harvest value (at market price): $______ * ROI: (Harvest value. Investment) ÷ Investment. Example: Invested $30, harvest worth $60 → ROI = 100% (doubled money)

description.en: Create written agreement: * "We agree that vegetables will be shared by: _____" * Options: equally, by contribution, by need, combination. All group members sign. Post agreements with garden designs
description.es: Create written agreement: * "We agree that vegetables will be shared by: _____" * Options: equally, by contribution, by need, combination. All group members sign. Post agreements with garden designs

description.en: View other groups' designs. Notice different solutions to fair distribution Investment Tracking Sheet Format: ``` COMMUNITY GARDEN INVESTMENT TRACKER Group Name: _____________________ CONTRIBUTIONS: Name Cash Seeds Tools Time TOTAL VALUE ____________ $___ $___ $___ $___ $______ ____________ $___ $___ $___ $___ $______ ____________ $___ $___ $___ $___ $______ ____________ $___ $___ $___ $___ $______ TOTAL GROUP INVESTMENT: $______ GOAL: $200 ✅ Met / ❌ Short by $____ PLOT ASSIGNMENTS: Name Plot Size (sq ft) Reason for Size _____________ ________ ______________ _____________ ________ ______________ SHARING AGREEMENT: We agree to share the harvest by: □ Equal shares for everyone □ Proportional to investment □ Based on need □ Other: _______________ Signed: _________________ _________________ _________________ _________________ _________________ _________________ ```
description.es: View other groups' designs. Notice different solutions to fair distribution Investment Tracking Sheet Format: ``` COMMUNITY GARDEN INVESTMENT TRACKER Group Name: _____________________ CONTRIBUTIONS: Name Cash Seeds Tools Time TOTAL VALUE ____________ $___ $___ $___ $___ $______ ____________ $___ $___ $___ $___ $______ ____________ $___ $___ $___ $___ $______ ____________ $___ $___ $___ $___ $______ TOTAL GROUP INVESTMENT: $______ GOAL: $200 ✅ Met / ❌ Short by $____ PLOT ASSIGNMENTS: Name Plot Size (sq ft) Reason for Size _____________ ________ ______________ _____________ ________ ______________ SHARING AGREEMENT: We agree to share the harvest by: □ Equal shares for everyone □ Proportional to investment □ Based on need □ Other: _______________ Signed: _________________ _________________ _________________ _________________ _________________ _________________ ```

discussionQuestions: Is it fair to give bigger plots to bigger investors, or should everyone get equal space?
What if someone contributed tools instead of money—should they get less vegetables?
How does a community garden help people who can't afford their own garden?
What's the return on investment if you invest $30 and get $60 worth of vegetables?
Could this idea work for other community projects? What else?

description.en: Show handmade bracelet and store-bought bracelet side-by-side. Discuss differences: "Which is unique? Which looks exactly like others?". Introduce concept: "Today you'll make something AND track how long it takes". Explain time tracking sheet
description.es: Show handmade bracelet and store-bought bracelet side-by-side. Discuss differences: "Which is unique? Which looks exactly like others?". Introduce concept: "Today you'll make something AND track how long it takes". Explain time tracking sheet

description.es: Students choose a simple craft project: * Beaded bracelet or necklace * Felt bookmark * Decorated card or frame. As they work, they track time on worksheet: * Start time: _____ * End time: _____ * Total minutes: _____. Teacher calls out 5-minute intervals

20.label: 20 Minutes

20.activityName: Value Beyond Price: Memory Art Project

description.en: Show two items: a dollar bill and a family photo. Ask: "Which can you buy? Which is priceless?". Explain: "Priceless means so special you could never buy it". Share: "Today we'll draw something priceless to you"
description.es: Show two items: a dollar bill and a family photo. Ask: "Which can you buy? Which is priceless?". Explain: "Priceless means so special you could never buy it". Share: "Today we'll draw something priceless to you"

description.en: Students draw something priceless to them: * A person they love (family member, friend, teacher, pet) * A special memory (birthday party, family trip, special day) * Something they treasure (not for its cost, but for meaning). Encourage detail and color. Circulate and ask: "Why is this priceless to you?"
description.es: Students draw something priceless to them: * A person they love (family member, friend, teacher, pet) * A special memory (birthday party, family trip, special day) * Something they treasure (not for its cost, but for meaning). materials: Quality art paper, card stock, or small canvases

description.en: Read short book or show images about Day of the Dead tradition. Discuss key concept: "People honor loved ones with priceless offerings—photos, favorite foods, treasured items". Introduce FL concept: Intrinsic Value * "Value that exists inside something, not based on money" * "Things that matter for what they ARE, not what they cost". Examples of priceless things: * People you love (can't buy family) * Memories (can't purchase experiences after they happen) * Cultural traditions (can't buy heritage) * Feelings (love, joy, connection). Students brainstorm: "What's priceless to you?"
description.es: Read short book or show images about Day of the Dead tradition. Discuss key concept: "People honor loved ones with priceless offerings—photos, favorite foods, treasured items". Introduce FL concept: Intrinsic Value * "Value that exists inside something, not based on money" * "Things that matter for what they ARE, not what they cost". Examples of priceless things: * People you love (can't buy family) * Memories (can't purchase experiences after they happen) * Cultural traditions (can't buy heritage) * Feelings (love, joy, connection). Students brainstorm: "What's priceless to you?"

description.en: Students create artwork honoring something priceless: * Theme A: Person who is priceless to me (family, friend, teacher, mentor) * Theme B: Memory that's priceless (special day, tradition, experience) * Theme C: Value that matters more than money (kindness, love, honesty, family). Use mixed media for depth: * Drawing/painting base * Collage elements * Written words incorporated * Symbolic representations. Quality encouraged: this is honoring something precious. Teacher circulates, asks guiding questions: "Why is this priceless? What does it represent?"
description.es: Students create artwork honoring something priceless: * Theme A: Person who is priceless to me (family, friend, teacher, mentor) * Theme B: Memory that's priceless (special day, tradition, experience) * Theme C: Value that matters more than money (kindness, love, honesty, family). description.en: Assign roles: * Vendors (60% of class): run booths * Shoppers (30%): browse and buy * Market Managers (10%): help resolve issues, make change, support - Booth Setup by Category: * Handmade Crafts Booth (CH10 items): beaded jewelry, ornaments, cards * Art Gallery (CH11 items): memory art (some for sale, some priceless/display only) * Garden Produce Stand: shared garden items, drawn or cut from paper. No real food. * Paper Goods Booth (cost of goods): paper treats — cookies, cupcakes and pretzels drawn and cut from card — each priced from what the card and the labor cost * Repair & Service Station (CH05): fix broken items, sharpen pencils, for fee * Trading Post (CH01): trade items without money. Vendors: * Price items (must justify: materials + labor, or fair trade value) * Arrange booth attractively * Create signs * Assign roles (cashier, sales, inventory)
description.es: Assign roles: * Vendors (60% of class): run booths * Shoppers (30%): browse and buy * Market Managers (10%): help resolve issues, make change, support - Booth Setup by Category: * Handmade Crafts Booth (CH10 items): beaded jewelry, ornaments, cards * Art Gallery (CH11 items): memory art (some for sale, some priceless/display only) * Garden Produce Stand: shared garden items, drawn or cut from paper. No real food. * Paper Goods Booth (cost of goods): paper treats — cookies, cupcakes and pretzels drawn and cut from card — each priced from what the card and the labor cost * Repair & Service Station (CH05): fix broken items, sharpen pencils, for fee * Trading Post (CH01): trade items without money. Vendors: * Price items (must justify: materials + labor, or fair trade value) * Arrange booth attractively * Create signs * Assign roles (cashier, sales, inventory)

description.en: Open market! Ring bell. Shoppers browse all booths. Make purchasing decisions. Vendors: * Sell items * Negotiate prices * Track inventory * Provide receipts. Market Managers circulate helping. Real market dynamics occur: * Some items sell out fast (demand!) * Perishables get discount as time passes (CH08) * Vendors adjust prices based on demand * Trades happen at Trading Post
description.es: Open market! Ring bell. Shoppers browse all booths. Make purchasing decisions. Vendors: * Sell items * Negotiate prices * Track inventory * Provide receipts. title.en: Measure Twice, Cut Once: Precision Building Challenge
title.es: Measure Twice, Cut Once: Precision Building Challenge

20.label: 20 Minutes
20.bestFor: Tight schedules, younger students (K-1), daily scheduling

description.en: Teacher shows careful folding technique. Emphasize: "Watch closely. Precision matters."
description.es: Teacher shows careful folding technique. Emphasize: "Watch closely. Precision matters."

description.en: Students follow instructions to fold paper into specific shape (paper airplane, origami cup, or simple box). Teacher circulates, doesn't intervene.
description.es: Students follow instructions to fold paper into specific shape (paper airplane, origami cup, or simple box). Teacher circulates, doesn't intervene.

description.en: Hold up results. Compare to teacher's model. How many match exactly? Discuss what happened when steps were rushed or measurements were off.
description.es: Hold up results. Compare to teacher's model. How many match exactly? Discuss what happened when steps were rushed or measurements were off.

description.en: "What happens if you don't measure/fold carefully?" Connect to: carpenters can't unfold wood once it's cut.
description.es: "What happens if you don't measure/fold carefully?" Connect to: carpenters can't unfold wood once it's cut.

discussionQuestions: Did your paper look like the example?
What happened if you folded in the wrong place?
Can you unfold and start over with paper? Can you with wood?

30.label: 30 Minutes
30.bestFor: Standard class periods, grades 1-3, weekly scheduling
materials: Cardboard sheets (one per student or pair)
Template with exact dimensions (e.g., "Cut rectangle: 4 inches x 6 inches")

description.en: Show template with measurements. Students must create exact rectangle by measuring and cutting. Review ruler use. Emphasize: "Measure twice, cut once."
description.es: Show template with measurements. Students must create exact rectangle by measuring and cutting. Review ruler use. Emphasize: "Measure twice, cut once."

description.en: Students measure carefully and mark cutting lines on cardboard. Teacher checks measurements before anyone cuts.
description.es: Students measure carefully and mark cutting lines on cardboard. Teacher checks measurements before anyone cuts.

description.en: Students cut along marked lines.
description.es: Students cut along marked lines.

description.en: Measure finished rectangles. Award "Precision Points" for pieces within 1/4 inch of target. Display results: how many were accurate?
description.es: Measure finished rectangles. Award "Precision Points" for pieces within 1/4 inch of target. Display results: how many were accurate?

description.en: Show pile of scrap cardboard. "This is waste. If cardboard costs $1 per sheet and we wasted 30% making mistakes, we spent $0.30 extra. In a business, that adds up." Calculate class waste.
description.es: Show pile of scrap cardboard. "This is waste. If cardboard costs $1 per sheet and we wasted 30% making mistakes, we spent $0.30 extra. In a business, that adds up." Calculate class waste.

discussionQuestions: How many got the exact measurements?
What mistakes did you make?
How much cardboard did we waste?
If you were selling these, would mistakes cost you money?
extensionIdeas: Build simple box from measured cardboard pieces—precision matters for fit.

45.label: 45 Minutes
materials: Rulers, pencils, scissors (or safe cutting tools)
"Materials budget" written on a scrap-paper card, crossed out and rewritten as it is spent
Waste tracking and cost calculation worksheets

description.en: Each team writes $10 at the top of a scrap-paper budget card; Cardboard costs $2 per sheet, crossed off the card at purchase; Challenge: Build structure to exact specifications (e.g., box that's 5"x5"x3"); Every mistake = buy new materials = less left on the card; Goal: Build to spec with minimal waste
description.es: Each team writes $10 at the top of a scrap-paper budget card; Cardboard costs $2 per sheet, crossed off the card at purchase; Challenge: Build structure to exact specifications (e.g., box that's 5"x5"x3"); Every mistake = buy new materials = less left on the card; Goal: Build to spec with minimal waste

description.en: Teams plan their cuts on paper first; Calculate how many pieces needed and measurements; Draw cutting diagram to minimize waste; Teacher approves plan before materials are distributed
description.es: Teams plan their cuts on paper first; Calculate how many pieces needed and measurements; Draw cutting diagram to minimize waste; Teacher approves plan before materials are distributed

description.en: Teams measure carefully, mark, and cut; Track every piece of waste on worksheet; Build structure according to specs; Teacher circulates, doesn't help—mistakes are learning
description.es: Teams measure carefully, mark, and cut; Track every piece of waste on worksheet; Build structure according to specs; Teacher circulates, doesn't help—mistakes are learning

description.en: Measure finished structures against specs; Award "precision points" for accuracy (within 1/4 inch = full points); Calculate waste: measure scrap pieces, tally total
description.es: Measure finished structures against specs; Award "precision points" for accuracy (within 1/4 inch = full points); Calculate waste: measure scrap pieces, tally total

description.en: Calculate cost: materials purchased, waste generated; If structure meets specs with minimal waste = "profit"; If excessive waste or structure doesn't meet specs = "loss"; Graph class results: waste % vs. success rate
description.es: Calculate cost: materials purchased, waste generated; If structure meets specs with minimal waste = "profit"; If excessive waste or structure doesn't meet specs = "loss"; Graph class results: waste % vs. success rate

discussionQuestions: "What was your biggest challenge in measuring precisely?"
"How much material did you waste? What did that cost?"
"If you could do it again, what would you change?"
"How does precision affect profit in real businesses?"
"Why do builders and carpenters measure so carefully?"
"What's the difference between 'good enough' and 'exact'?"
extensionIdeas: Second round with same challenge—track improvement
Design your own structure and create specs for others to build
Calculate % waste across class—what's acceptable? What's too much?
Research: how do real factories minimize waste?
Visit hardware store to price materials and understand real costs

description.es: Discuss packaging: protects product, makes it attractive, tells information. Show examples of good packaging. Explain design challenge: create package for a simple product.

description.en: Students choose a simple product to package (real or pretend): toy, craft, food item. Sketch package ideas. Plan: What shape? What information? What colors? How to make it attractive?
description.es: Students choose a simple product to package (real or pretend): toy, craft, food item. Sketch package ideas. Plan: What shape? What information? What colors? How to make it attractive?

description.es: Students draw detailed package design on paper: all sides, labels, how it opens. Include product name and key information.

description.es: Students present packages in small groups. Explain design choices: Why this shape? What makes it attractive? What information is important? Get peer feedback on design.

description.es: Students complete worksheet: What's your brand name? (can be your own name + "Creations"). Sketch simple logo. Choose 2-3 brand colors.

description.es: Fold pre-scored boxes or assemble simple boxes from template.

description.es: Transfer brand name and logo to box. Use brand colors. Add decorative elements. Make it look "store quality."

description.es: Create complete brand identity: business name, tagline, logo, color palette; Design packaging that reflects brand; Consider target customer: "Who will buy this? What do they like?"

description.en: Calculate packaging costs: plain box = $0.50, decoration supplies = $0.25-1.00 depending on use; Compare: product alone vs. in plain box vs. in branded box; Estimate: "What could I charge for each version?"; Discuss: packaging cost vs. increased perceived value—worth it?
description.es: Calculate packaging costs: plain box = $0.50, decoration supplies = $0.25-1.00 depending on use; Compare: product alone vs. in plain box vs. in branded box; Estimate: "What could I charge for each version?"; Discuss: packaging cost vs. increased perceived value—worth it?

description.en: 4-5 students present their packaged product to class (1 min each); Explain brand choices and target customer; Class feedback: would you buy it? Does packaging match product?
description.es: 4-5 students present their packaged product to class (1 min each); Explain brand choices and target customer; Class feedback: would you buy it? Does packaging match product?

description.en: Introduce clay: what it is, how it's used, why makers use it. Demonstrate basic techniques: rolling, pinching, smoothing. Review clay safety: wet hands, gentle handling, cleanup procedures.
description.es: Introduce clay: what it is, how it's used, why makers use it. Demonstrate basic techniques: rolling, pinching, smoothing. Review clay safety: wet hands, gentle handling, cleanup procedures.

description.en: Students explore clay through play: squeeze, roll into balls, make coils (snakes), flatten into pancakes. Get familiar with how clay feels and moves. Experiment with basic shapes.
description.es: Students explore clay through play: squeeze, roll into balls, make coils (snakes), flatten into pancakes. Get familiar with how clay feels and moves. Experiment with basic shapes.

description.en: Students create simple clay object: bowl, animal, cup, or decorative item. Practice techniques: pinching to shape, smoothing cracks, joining pieces. Work carefully and thoughtfully.
description.es: Students create simple clay object: bowl, animal, cup, or decorative item. Practice techniques: pinching to shape, smoothing cracks, joining pieces. Work carefully and thoughtfully.

description.en: Students add details to their clay creation: texture with tools, carved patterns, smoothed surfaces. Refine shape and appearance. Prepare for drying.
description.es: Students add details to their clay creation: texture with tools, carved patterns, smoothed surfaces. Refine shape and appearance. Prepare for drying.

description.en: Students display their clay creations for gallery walk. Discuss: What was challenging about clay? What techniques worked? How is clay different from other art materials? What would you make next time?
description.es: Students display their clay creations for gallery walk. Discuss: What was challenging about clay? What techniques worked? How is clay different from other art materials? What would you make next time?

discussionQuestions: Was it easy or hard to shape clay?
Did your bowl turn out perfect?
What would happen if you practiced every day?

30.label: 30 Minutes
30.bestFor: Standard class periods, grades 1-3, weekly scheduling
30.activityName: Guided Clay Project with Value Discussion
materials: Air-dry clay or playdough (sufficient for each student to make 2-3 small items)
Simple tools (popsicle sticks, plastic knives, straws for texture)
Optional: water in small cups for smoothing

description.en: Examine different clay types. Brief discussion: people have made things from clay for thousands of years. Why? It's free from the earth, moldable, and useful.
description.es: Examine different clay types. Brief discussion: people have made things from clay for thousands of years. Why? It's free from the earth, moldable, and useful.

description.en: Demonstrate 3-4 techniques: pinch pot, coil building, slab construction, and stamp texturing. Students practice each briefly before choosing their project.
description.es: Demonstrate 3-4 techniques: pinch pot, coil building, slab construction, and stamp texturing. Students practice each briefly before choosing their project.

description.en: Students create their chosen project using learned techniques. Encourage adding details and personal touches. Teacher circulates to support and challenge.
description.es: Students create their chosen project using learned techniques. Encourage adding details and personal touches. Teacher circulates to support and challenge.

description.en: Discuss: How much would this cost to buy in a store? How much did our materials cost? Calculate the value of skill — your hands and knowledge turned cheap clay into something valuable.
description.es: Discuss: How much would this cost to buy in a store? How much did our materials cost? Calculate the value of skill — your hands and knowledge turned cheap clay into something valuable.

description.en: Display all creations. Students assign a fair price to their work considering materials, time, and skill. Compare: Why are handmade items often more expensive than factory-made?
description.es: Display all creations. Students assign a fair price to their work considering materials, time, and skill. Compare: Why are handmade items often more expensive than factory-made?

description.en: Share one thing learned about how skill adds value to raw materials. Clean up workspace and set projects to dry.
description.es: Share one thing learned about how skill adds value to raw materials. Clean up workspace and set projects to dry.

discussionQuestions: Did your second attempt turn out better than your first?
How does practice change the value of what you make?
If clay costs $1 but a skilled potter spends an hour making a beautiful bowl, what should they charge?
Why do handmade pottery items cost more than plastic bowls?

description.es: Demonstrate 3 techniques: pinch pot, coil bowl, slab tile; Students try each briefly (3-4 min per technique); Take mental note of which feels most natural

But my item 3 is much better quality—could I charge $5 for it?"; Discuss: skilled potters charge $20-100 for bowls. Why? (Years of practice = high skill = high value)
description.es: Clay cost: $0.50 per item; Time investment: [varies by student]; Calculate: "If I charge $1 per hour for my time, item 1 costs $__ [clay + time]. description.en: Divide class in half. Each side is a store selling the same items (pencils, erasers, bookmarks). Both stores set same prices. Emphasize: prices are identical.
description.es: Divide class in half. Each side is a store selling the same items (pencils, erasers, bookmarks). Both stores set same prices. Emphasize: prices are identical.

description.en: Give stores 3 minutes to make their store different WITHOUT changing prices. Options: better signs, friendly greeting, organized display, sample item, etc.
description.es: Give stores 3 minutes to make their store different WITHOUT changing prices. Options: better signs, friendly greeting, organized display, sample item, etc.

description.en: Teacher and volunteers act as customers, each carrying 8 paper clips as coins. Customers choose which store to visit. Stores track how many customers they get. No price changes allowed.
description.es: Teacher and volunteers act as customers, each carrying 8 paper clips as coins. Customers choose which store to visit. Stores track how many customers they get. No price changes allowed.

description.en: Count customers for each store. Discuss: Which store got more customers? Why? What made you choose one store over the other? List factors on board.
description.es: Count customers for each store. Discuss: Which store got more customers? Why? What made you choose one store over the other? List factors on board.

discussionQuestions: What happened to profit in Round 1 when everyone kept lowering prices?
What differentiations did teams add in Round 2?
Would you pay more for something if it came with a guarantee or was made just for you?
How is this like the story where Neville's cheap shelf fell, but Ellis's quality work lasted?
What does 'competitive advantage' mean?

45.label: 45 Minutes
materials: Paper clips as coins — 10 per customer — collected back and reused
Product materials (craft supplies, printed "goods," or menus)
Chart paper for data tracking and graphing

description.en: Divide class into 6-8 competing businesses selling similar products. Each team gets identical starting inventory and an empty cup for the paper clips they take in. Explain: you must attract customers away from competitors.
description.es: Divide class into 6-8 competing businesses selling similar products. Each team gets identical starting inventory and an empty cup for the paper clips they take in. Explain: you must attract customers away from competitors.

description.en: Teams can only compete on price. Customers (rotating students) shop for best deals. Track sales. Debrief: What happened to prices? (Race to the bottom.) Did anyone make profit?
description.es: Teams can only compete on price. Customers (rotating students) shop for best deals. Track sales. Debrief: What happened to prices? (Race to the bottom.) Did anyone make profit?

description.en: Now teams can change their product — add features, improve packaging, offer bundles, create loyalty cards. Same shopping period. Track sales and compare to Round 1.
description.es: Now teams can change their product — add features, improve packaging, offer bundles, create loyalty cards. Same shopping period. Track sales and compare to Round 1.

description.en: Teams can use price, differentiation, AND customer service. Introduce advertising (30-second pitches). Final shopping round. Track all transactions.
description.es: Teams can use price, differentiation, AND customer service. Introduce advertising (30-second pitches). Final shopping round. Track all transactions.

description.en: Calculate profit/loss for each round. Chart class results. Discuss: Which strategy worked best? Why do some businesses succeed while others fail? What made customers switch?
description.es: Calculate profit/loss for each round. Chart class results. Discuss: Which strategy worked best? Why do some businesses succeed while others fail? What made customers switch?

description.en: Name two real businesses that compete with each other. How do they differentiate? Write one lesson learned about competition that you could use if you started a business.
description.es: Name two real businesses that compete with each other. How do they differentiate? Write one lesson learned about competition that you could use if you started a business.

discussionQuestions: In Round 1, what happened to businesses that just kept lowering prices?
Give an example of a differentiation strategy a team used.
Did customers care about differentiation, or did they only want the cheapest option?
How is profit margin different from total revenue?
Connect to the story: Why did Ellis decide to RAISE prices instead of lowering them?
What was Maplewood Makers' competitive advantage? (Quality, guarantees, customer relationships)
Real world: Can you think of businesses that charge MORE but people still buy from them? (Apple, Starbucks, etc.) Why?
What's the risk of always being the cheapest option in your market?
extensionIdeas: Research real-world examples of differentiation (Southwest Airlines: friendly service; Volvo: safety; In-N-Out Burger: fresh ingredients)
Create advertising campaigns highlighting each team's competitive advantage
Write business case studies: "When [Team Name] competed on price, profit was $X. When they differentiated with [strategy], profit became $Y."
Graph long-term scenarios: "If you make $1 profit per item vs. $4 profit per item, how many must you sell to earn $100?"
Debate: "Should businesses ever compete primarily on price? When might that strategy make sense?"

45.label: 45 Minutes

materials: Bulk buying comparison cards (small pack vs. large pack with prices)
Paper clips as coins for the demonstration
PROFIT jar and COSTS jar (labeled containers)
Chart paper for class overhead tracking

description.en: Introduce detailed lemonade stand scenario with price list. Students will track ALL costs including ones people forget. Review terms: revenue, expenses, overhead, profit.
description.es: Introduce detailed lemonade stand scenario with price list. Students will track ALL costs including ones people forget. Review terms: revenue, expenses, overhead, profit.

description.en: Break costs into categories: Direct costs (lemons, sugar, cups), Overhead (table rental, sign materials), Labor (your time). Students brainstorm items in each category.
description.es: Break costs into categories: Direct costs (lemons, sugar, cups), Overhead (table rental, sign materials), Labor (your time). Students brainstorm items in each category.

description.en: In pairs, students estimate real costs for each item using provided price sheet. Calculate total direct costs, total overhead, total labor. Record in cost tracking worksheet.
description.es: In pairs, students estimate real costs for each item using provided price sheet. Calculate total direct costs, total overhead, total labor. Record in cost tracking worksheet.

description.en: Compare costs: buying 10 lemons individually vs. bag of 10. Calculate savings. Discuss: Why is bulk cheaper? What's the catch? (need money upfront, might waste extra)
description.es: Compare costs: buying 10 lemons individually vs. bag of 10. Calculate savings. Discuss: Why is bulk cheaper? What's the catch? (need money upfront, might waste extra)

description.en: Students design a simple tracking sheet to log hidden costs. Categories: Supplies, Time, Overhead. Practice filling it out for lemonade stand.
description.es: Students design a simple tracking sheet to log hidden costs. Categories: Supplies, Time, Overhead. Practice filling it out for lemonade stand.

description.en: Calculate final profit: Revenue - Direct Costs - Overhead - Labor = Profit. Compare to original guess. Discuss: What surprised you? How can businesses reduce hidden costs?
description.es: Calculate final profit: Revenue - Direct Costs - Overhead - Labor = Profit. Compare to original guess. Discuss: What surprised you? How can businesses reduce hidden costs?

discussionQuestions: What's the difference between overhead and material costs?
Why do we need a RESERVE jar for future tool replacement?
How does bulk buying change your true cost over time?
What happens to businesses that don't count hidden costs?
Is it 'bad' to discover hidden costs? Or is it helpful to know the truth?
How much overhead should we add to our prices? 10%? 20%? How do we decide?

description.en: Discuss business challenge: when you get too many orders at once. Explain simulation: students will receive multiple task cards at once and must decide what to do first. Review concepts: priority, delegation, time management.
description.es: Discuss business challenge: when you get too many orders at once. Explain simulation: students will receive multiple task cards at once and must decide what to do first. Review concepts: priority, delegation, time management.

description.en: Students receive stack of task cards (simple classroom tasks: organize bookshelf, sharpen pencils, sort papers, etc.). Read all tasks. Decide: Which is most urgent? Which takes longest? Which should go first? Make priority list.
description.es: Students receive stack of task cards (simple classroom tasks: organize bookshelf, sharpen pencils, sort papers, etc.). Read all tasks. Decide: Which is most urgent? Which takes longest? Which should go first? Make priority list.

description.en: Students work through their tasks in priority order. Set timer. Try to complete as many as possible. If working in pairs, practice delegating: 'You do this one, I'll do that one.' Track what gets done.
description.es: Students work through their tasks in priority order. Set timer. Try to complete as many as possible. If working in pairs, practice delegating: 'You do this one, I'll do that one.' Track what gets done.

description.es: Each student gets 8-10 task cards (draw, fold, sort, count, write, build). Timer starts — complete as many as possible alone in 4 minutes. Count completed tasks.

description.es: Same tasks, but now in teams of 3-4. Assign roles based on skills. Timer starts — how many more tasks get completed? Compare solo vs. team results.

title.en: Slow Season Strategy: What Do Smart Businesses Do?

description.en: Teams complete comprehensive "Slow Season Action Plan": **PART 1: Understanding the Problem** Current situation (how much money coming in now vs. busy season?) How long will slow season last? Do we have reserve funds? How much? **PART 2: Survival Strategies** What can we PREPARE for next busy season? (build inventory, make products, plan marketing) What can we IMPROVE right now? (fix equipment, reorganize, train skills) What can we LEARN to get better? (take classes, practice, research) What RELATIONSHIPS can we strengthen? (call past customers, thank people, ask for referrals) Can we offer a DIFFERENT product for this season? (pivot: pool company offers hot tub service, pumpkin farm hosts winter events) **PART 3: Budget Planning** Use reserve funds: Yes or No? How much? Cut expenses: What can wait? Investments worth making: What will help later?
description.es: Teams complete comprehensive "Slow Season Action Plan": **PART 1: Understanding the Problem** Current situation (how much money coming in now vs. busy season?) How long will slow season last? Do we have reserve funds? How much? **PART 2: Survival Strategies** What can we PREPARE for next busy season? (build inventory, make products, plan marketing) What can we IMPROVE right now? (fix equipment, reorganize, train skills) What can we LEARN to get better? (take classes, practice, research) What RELATIONSHIPS can we strengthen? (call past customers, thank people, ask for referrals) Can we offer a DIFFERENT product for this season? (pivot: pool company offers hot tub service, pumpkin farm hosts winter events) **PART 3: Budget Planning** Use reserve funds: Yes or No? How much? Cut expenses: What can wait? Investments worth making: What will help later?

discussionQuestions: What's the difference between a failing business and a business in slow season?
Why is giving up during slow season a bad idea?
How can slow times actually be GOOD for a business?
What does 'the roots are growing underground' mean for business? (Frances's garden metaphor)
Why did Ms. Rivera call? How did something the team did in November help them in January? (relationship building)
What's an emergency fund and why do businesses need one?
Can you think of businesses in our community that have slow seasons? What do they do?
How is 'slow season' different from 'no one wants your product'?
